subject: Biology
text: (a) A woman with blood group O married a man with blood group AB. Show the possible blood groups of the progeny. List the alleles involved in this inheritance. modelAnswer: (a) Blood group is controlled by multiple alleles I^A, I^B and i. Mother (O) genotype = ii; Father (AB) genotype = I^A I^B. Cross: ii x I^A I^B gives offspring genotypes I^A i and I^B i in equal proportion, i.e. 50% blood group A (I^A i) and 50% blood group B (I^B i). None of the children will have blood group O or AB.
keyPoints: Alleles involved: I^A, I^B, i
ii x I^A I^B -> 1/2 I^A i (group A) : 1/2 I^B i (group B)
No child has group O or AB

text: [OR] If the mother is a carrier of colour blindness and the father is normal, show the possible genotype and phenotype of the offspring of the next generation, with the help of a Punnett square.
modelAnswer: Colour blindness is an X-linked recessive trait. Mother (carrier) genotype = X^C X^c; Father (normal) genotype = X^C Y. Punnett square cross X^C X^c x X^C Y gives offspring: X^C X^C (normal daughter), X^C X^c (carrier daughter), X^C Y (normal son), X^c Y (colour-blind son). Thus 50% of daughters are carriers (none colour-blind) and 50% of sons are colour-blind.
keyPoints: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive
X^C X^c x X^C Y -> 1/4 normal daughter, 1/4 carrier daughter, 1/4 normal son, 1/4 colour-blind son
All daughters phenotypically normal; half the sons colour-blind

subject: Biology
text: Explain gene therapy, with reference to treatment of SCID.
modelAnswer: Gene therapy is a technique used to correct a genetic defect by inserting a normal, functional gene into the cells or tissue of an individual to compensate for a defective/non-functional gene. In SCID (Severe Combined Immuno-Deficiency, caused by a deficiency of the enzyme adenosine deaminase, ADA), lymphocytes are extracted from the patient's bone marrow, and a normal, functional copy of the ADA gene is introduced into these cells using a retroviral vector. These genetically corrected lymphocytes are then returned to the patient's body, where they produce ADA enzyme, restoring normal immune function. Since these lymphocytes are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusions unless the corrected gene is introduced into bone marrow stem cells for a permanent cure.
keyPoints: Gene therapy = correcting genetic defect by inserting a normal gene
SCID caused by ADA gene deficiency
Lymphocytes from patient are corrected with functional ADA gene via a vector and reinfused

subject: Biology
text: Explain industrial melanism.
modelAnswer: Industrial melanism is an example of natural selection observed in the peppered moth (Biston betularia) in industrialized areas of England. Before industrialization, light-coloured moths were more common as they were camouflaged against lichen-covered light tree barks, while dark (melanic) moths were easily seen and eaten by predators. After industrialization, soot and pollution darkened the tree trunks (killing lichens), so dark moths became better camouflaged and survived better, while light moths became conspicuous and were preyed upon. As a result, the frequency of the dark-coloured melanic form increased in polluted industrial areas, demonstrating natural selection in action in response to environmental change.
keyPoints: Peppered moth (Biston betularia) example
Soot darkened tree barks favoured dark (melanic) moths via better camouflage

subject: Biology
text: Describe the tissue culture technique in plants.
modelAnswer: Plant tissue culture is the technique of growing isolated plant cells, tissues or organs (explants) aseptically on an artificial nutrient medium under controlled conditions to regenerate a whole new plant. Steps: 1. A small piece of tissue (explant) is taken from a healthy plant and surface sterilized. 2. It is cultured on a nutrient medium (containing sugars, minerals, vitamins and plant growth hormones like auxins and cytokinins) in aseptic conditions. 3. The explant proliferates into an undifferentiated mass of cells called callus. 4. By altering the hormone concentration (auxin:cytokinin ratio) in the medium, the callus is induced to differentiate into shoots and roots (organogenesis) or somatic embryos (somatic embryogenesis). 5. The regenerated plantlets are hardened and transferred to soil. This technique allows rapid clonal propagation of genetically identical, disease-free plants.
keyPoints: Explant cultured aseptically on nutrient medium with hormones (auxin, cytokinin)
Forms an undifferentiated callus
Hormone ratio controls differentiation into shoots/roots (organogenesis)
Produces disease-free, genetically identical clones rapidly

subject: Biology
text: Describe post transcriptional processing of RNA in eukaryotes.
modelAnswer: In eukaryotes, the primary transcript (hnRNA) formed by transcription is non-functional and undergoes post-transcriptional processing before it becomes a mature, functional mRNA. This processing involves three main steps: 1. Capping: A 7-methyl guanosine cap (5' cap) is added to the 5' end of the hnRNA. This cap protects the mRNA from degradation and is needed for ribosome binding during translation. 2. Tailing: A poly-A tail (a chain of adenylate residues, typically 100-200) is added at the 3' end of the hnRNA. This tail provides stability to the mRNA. 3. Splicing: Eukaryotic genes are split/interrupted - they contain coding sequences called exons and non-coding intervening sequences called introns. During splicing, the introns are precisely removed from the hnRNA and the exons are joined together in the correct sequence to form mature mRNA. Only after capping, tailing and splicing does the hnRNA become functional, mature mRNA that can be transported out of the nucleus for translation.
keyPoints: hnRNA (primary transcript) undergoes capping, tailing and splicing
Capping: 7-methyl guanosine cap added at 5' end - protects mRNA, aids ribosome binding
Tailing: poly-A tail added at 3' end - provides stability
Splicing: introns removed, exons joined to form mature mRNA

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Describe Avery, McLeod and McCarty's experiment. State its significance.
modelAnswer: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) worked to identify the biochemical nature of the 'transforming principle' discovered earlier by Griffith in pneumococcus bacteria. They purified biochemicals (proteins, DNA, RNA) from heat-killed virulent (S strain, smooth) Streptococcus pneumoniae and treated each separately with the non-virulent live R strain (rough) bacteria. They found that: 1. Digesting the extract with proteases (to destroy proteins) or RNase (to destroy RNA) did not stop transformation - R strain bacteria still transformed into S strain. 2. Digesting the extract with DNase (to destroy DNA) did stop the transformation - R strain bacteria remained non-virulent. This proved that DNA, and not protein or RNA, was the genetic/transforming material responsible for converting the harmless R strain into the virulent S strain. Significance: This experiment provided the first direct biochemical evidence that DNA (and not protein) is the genetic material responsible for heredity, laying the foundation for molecular genetics.
keyPoints: Purified biochemicals from S-strain pneumococcus tested on R-strain bacteria
Protease/RNase treatment did not stop transformation; DNase treatment did
Proved DNA (not protein) is the transforming/genetic material
First direct biochemical proof that DNA is the genetic material

subject: Biology
text: Write a short note on Chipko Movement.
modelAnswer: The Chipko Movement was a grassroots forest conservation movement that began in 1973 in the Garhwal Himalayas (Uttarakhand, then part of Uttar Pradesh), started by local villagers led by figures such as Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt. Villagers, especially women, physically hugged/embraced ('chipko' means 'to stick/hug' in Hindi) trees to prevent them from being felled by contractors for commercial logging. The movement was based on the ancient Bishnoi tradition of tree protection and used non-violent Gandhian methods of resistance (satyagraha). The movement successfully stopped deforestation in the region, led to a 15-year ban on green felling in Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh by the government, and raised nationwide awareness about the importance of forest conservation, ecological balance, and community/women's participation in environmental protection. It became a model for community-based conservation movements across India.
keyPoints: Started 1973 in Garhwal Himalayas by villagers (Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt)
Villagers hugged trees to prevent felling by contractors
Non-violent Gandhian method of protest
Led to a ban on green felling in the region and raised environmental awareness nationwide

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Write a short note on Joint Forest Management.
modelAnswer: Joint Forest Management (JFM) is a government policy/programme, formally introduced in India in 1990, in which local village communities and the State Forest Department jointly protect, manage and share the benefits of nearby forest resources. Under this scheme, village-level institutions called Forest Protection Committees are formed; the community protects the forest from illegal felling, grazing and fires, and in return receives a share of the produce such as timber, fuelwood, fodder and non-timber forest products (fruits, resins, etc.), along with employment opportunities. The programme is based on the principle that local communities who depend on forests for their livelihood are best positioned to protect and sustainably manage them. JFM has helped in regenerating degraded forest land, reducing conflicts between forest departments and local people, and improving the socio-economic condition of forest-dependent communities while conserving biodiversity.
keyPoints: JFM: partnership between Forest Department and local village communities (from 1990)
Village Forest Protection Committees protect forests from felling/grazing/fire

subject: Biology
text: What does PCR stand for? Describe the different steps of PCR.
modelAnswer: PCR stands for Polymerase Chain Reaction, an in vitro technique used to amplify (produce multiple copies of) a specific segment of DNA rapidly. It involves repeated cycles, each having three steps: 1. Denaturation: The double-stranded DNA template is heated to about 94-96 degrees C, causing the two strands to separate into single strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds. 2. Annealing: The temperature is lowered to about 50-65 degrees C, allowing two short, specific single-stranded DNA primers to bind (hybridize) to their complementary sequences on the separated template strands, flanking the region to be amplified. 3. Extension (Elongation): The temperature is raised to about 72 degrees C, the optimum for the heat-stable DNA polymerase enzyme (Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus), which extends the primers by adding complementary nucleotides, synthesizing new complementary DNA strands. This three-step cycle is repeated 20-30 times in a thermal cycler, and since each cycle doubles the number of DNA copies, millions of copies of the target DNA sequence are produced within a few hours.
keyPoints: PCR = Polymerase Chain Reaction; amplifies specific DNA in vitro
Denaturation (~94 C): DNA strands separate
Annealing (~50-65 C): primers bind to template
Extension (~72 C): Taq polymerase synthesizes new strand; cycle repeated ~30 times for exponential amplification

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Give an account of the Blue-White Method of selection of recombinants.
modelAnswer: The Blue-White selection method is used to distinguish recombinant bacterial colonies (containing a foreign DNA insert) from non-recombinant colonies after a cloning experiment, using the vector pBR322/pUC-type plasmids that carry the lacZ gene fragment (encoding beta-galactosidase) with a restriction site inserted within it (insertional inactivation). The foreign DNA of interest is ligated into this restriction site within the lacZ gene. When bacteria are transformed and plated on a medium containing the chromogenic substrate X-gal (5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-beta-D-galactoside) along with an inducer, the following occurs: 1. If the recombinant DNA (foreign gene insert) has been successfully inserted into the lacZ gene, it disrupts/inactivates the gene, so beta-galactosidase is not produced; these bacterial colonies cannot hydrolyse X-gal and hence appear white - these are the recombinant colonies. 2. If there is no insert (i.e. the plasmid recircularized without the foreign DNA), the lacZ gene remains intact/functional, beta-galactosidase is produced, X-gal is hydrolysed to a blue coloured product, and the colonies appear blue - these are non-recombinant colonies. Thus, recombinants can be easily and rapidly identified visually by their white colour, distinguishing them from blue non-recombinant colonies.
keyPoints: Uses insertional inactivation of the lacZ gene (beta-galactosidase) on the vector
Foreign DNA insert disrupts lacZ - colony cannot cleave X-gal - appears WHITE (recombinant)
No insert - lacZ intact - cleaves X-gal - appears BLUE (non-recombinant)
Allows rapid visual screening of recombinant colonies

text: Define: Carrying capacity.
modelAnswer: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size of a species that a given habitat/environment can sustain indefinitely, given the availability of food, space and other resources, without degrading the environment.

subject: Biology

modelAnswer: Homologous chromosomes are a pair of chromosomes (one inherited from each parent) that are similar in size, shape, centromere position and carry genes for the same traits at corresponding loci.
keyPoints: Homologous chromosomes: matching pair, one from each parent, same gene loci

text: Give a reason: Bagging is essential in artificial hybridisation.
modelAnswer: Bagging (covering the emasculated flower with a bag) is essential in artificial hybridization to prevent contamination of the stigma with unwanted/foreign pollen carried by wind, insects, or other agents, thereby ensuring that only the desired pollen (applied later) fertilizes the flower.
keyPoints: Bagging prevents contamination by unwanted foreign pollen
Ensures only the desired cross-pollination occurs

subject: Biology
text: Give a reason: Climax stage is achieved quickly in secondary succession as compared to primary succession.
modelAnswer: Secondary succession occurs in areas where a pre-existing community was destroyed (e.g. by fire, flood or cultivation) but the soil with its nutrients, seeds and microorganisms already exists. Since the substratum is already fertile/well-formed, unlike bare rock in primary succession, colonization and development of vegetation proceed much faster, so the climax community is reached more quickly.
keyPoints: Secondary succession starts on an already-formed, nutrient-rich soil with seed bank
No need to build soil from scratch (as in primary succession on bare rock), so climax is reached faster

subject: Biology
text: What is a single cell protein? How is it significant for human welfare?

Rapidly produced, inexpensive source of protein that helps combat malnutrition

subject: Biology
text: What is reproductive fitness? Explain it with the help of an example.
modelAnswer: Reproductive fitness (Darwinian fitness) is the ability of an organism to survive and successfully produce fertile offspring that themselves survive to reproduce, under a given set of environmental conditions; individuals better adapted to their environment have higher reproductive fitness. Example: Among a population of peppered moths, dark-coloured moths in a soot-polluted (industrial) area are better camouflaged from predators than light-coloured moths, hence they survive longer and produce more offspring - so dark moths have higher reproductive fitness in that environment.
keyPoints: Reproductive fitness = ability to survive and produce fertile, surviving offspring
Example: dark peppered moths have higher fitness in polluted (sooty) habitats due to camouflage

subject: Biology
text: Give one significant difference between primary lymphoid organs and secondary lymphoid organs. Give one example of each.
modelAnswer: Primary lymphoid organs are the sites where lymphocytes (T-cells and B-cells) are produced and mature/differentiate (e.g. bone marrow and thymus), whereas secondary lymphoid organs are the sites where mature lymphocytes interact with antigens and proliferate into effector cells to mount an immune response (e.g. spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils).
keyPoints: Primary lymphoid organs: site of lymphocyte production/maturation, e.g. bone marrow, thymus
Secondary lymphoid organs: site of lymphocyte-antigen interaction and immune response, e.g. spleen, lymph nodes

subject: Biology
text: (a) Explain the term biofortification. How is this technique useful for the production of golden rice? [OR] (b) Write a short note on Electrophoresis.
modelAnswer: (a) Biofortification is the process of breeding/genetically engineering food crops to increase their nutritional value, such as content of proteins, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats, in order to combat malnutrition. Golden Rice: Rice does not naturally produce beta-carotene (a precursor of vitamin A) in its endosperm. Through biofortification (genetic engineering), genes for beta-carotene biosynthesis were introduced into rice, producing 'Golden Rice' which is rich in vitamin A precursor, helping to combat vitamin A deficiency, a major cause of blindness in children in developing countries.
keyPoints: Biofortification = breeding/engineering crops for higher nutrient content
Golden Rice was genetically engineered to produce beta-carotene (provitamin A) in the endosperm
Helps combat vitamin A deficiency/blindness

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Write a short note on Electrophoresis.
modelAnswer: Electrophoresis is a technique used to separate DNA, RNA or protein fragments based on their size/molecular weight and charge. The molecules (e.g. DNA fragments, which are negatively charged due to phosphate groups) are loaded into wells of a gel (usually agarose for DNA) and an electric current is passed through the gel. Since DNA is negatively charged, the fragments migrate towards the positive electrode (anode); smaller fragments move faster and travel farther through the gel matrix than larger fragments. After the run, the separated fragments are visualized as distinct bands by staining with a dye (e.g. ethidium bromide) under UV light. This technique is widely used in DNA fingerprinting, restriction mapping, and analysing PCR products.
keyPoints: Separates DNA/protein fragments by size and charge in a gel matrix under an electric field
DNA migrates toward the anode; smaller fragments move faster/farther
Bands visualized with a dye (e.g. ethidium bromide) under UV light
Used in DNA fingerprinting and restriction mapping

subject: Biology
text: Explain the evolution of long neck of giraffe according to Charles Darwin.
modelAnswer: According to Darwin's theory of natural selection, the ancestral giraffe population showed natural variation in neck length - some individuals had longer necks than others. During periods of food scarcity, individuals with longer necks could reach and browse foliage higher up on trees that shorter-necked individuals could not access. As a result, long-necked giraffes had a survival advantage, survived better, and produced more offspring, passing the long-neck trait to the next generation (differential reproduction). Over successive generations, through this continuous process of natural selection favouring longer necks, the average neck length of the giraffe population gradually increased, eventually giving rise to the modern long-necked giraffe. (This is in contrast to Lamarck's explanation, which proposed use and disuse/inheritance of acquired characters.)
keyPoints: Natural variation in neck length existed in ancestral giraffe population
Longer necks gave a survival advantage in accessing high foliage during food scarcity
Long-necked individuals survived and reproduced more (differential reproduction)
Over generations, natural selection increased average neck length - Darwin's mechanism, unlike Lamarck's use/disuse theory

subject: Biology
text: Describe the structure of a nucleosome.
modelAnswer: A nucleosome is the fundamental, repeating structural unit of chromatin in eukaryotes. Each nucleosome consists of a core of eight histone protein molecules (an octamer made of two molecules each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4). Around this histone octamer, a segment of DNA (about 200 base pairs) is wrapped in about 1.65 left-handed superhelical turns. Adjacent nucleosomes are connected/linked by a short stretch of linker DNA, and a fifth histone, H1, sits on the linker DNA and helps in packaging/condensing the nucleosome chain into higher-order chromatin structures. Under an electron microscope, this repeating structure of nucleosomes connected by linker DNA gives chromatin the appearance of 'beads on a string'.
keyPoints: Nucleosome = histone octamer (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) core
~200 bp DNA wrapped around the octamer in ~1.65 turns
Nucleosomes connected by linker DNA; H1 histone associates with linker DNA
Gives chromatin a 'beads-on-a-string' appearance

subject: Biology
text: Explain the Rivet Popper hypothesis.
modelAnswer: The Rivet Popper hypothesis, proposed by Paul Ehrlich, uses an analogy to explain the significance of biodiversity/species richness for ecosystem stability. It compares an aeroplane to an ecosystem, and the rivets holding it together to the various species in the ecosystem. Just as removing a single rivet at a time (a rivet popper randomly popping out rivets) may not immediately cause the plane to fail, but the plane becomes progressively weaker and less safe, until the loss of a critical rivet leads to sudden failure/crash of the plane - similarly, the loss of individual species (even seemingly unimportant ones) from an ecosystem may not have an immediate visible effect, but progressively weakens the ecosystem's ability to function; beyond a certain threshold, the loss of a keystone species can lead to a sudden collapse of the whole ecosystem. This hypothesis emphasizes that every species, however insignificant it may seem, has a role in maintaining ecosystem stability, hence highlighting the importance of conserving all species/biodiversity.
keyPoints: Ehrlich's analogy: species in an ecosystem = rivets holding an aeroplane together
Losing rivets/species one by one weakens the system without immediate collapse
Beyond a threshold, loss of a critical species causes sudden ecosystem collapse
Emphasizes importance of conserving all species, not just prominent ones

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Define: (1) Standing crop (2) Stenothermal organisms (3) Niche.
modelAnswer: (1) Standing crop: The total biomass (amount of living matter) or number of organisms present at a particular trophic level in an ecosystem at any given point in time. (2) Stenothermal organisms: Organisms that can tolerate/survive only a narrow range of temperature. (3) Niche: The complete functional role and position of a species within its habitat/ecosystem, including its habitat, food requirements, interactions with other species and its role in energy/nutrient flow (its 'address and profession' in the ecosystem).
keyPoints: Standing crop = biomass/number of organisms at a trophic level at a given time
Stenothermal organisms tolerate only a narrow temperature range
Niche = complete functional role and position of a species in its ecosystem

subject: Biology
text: Explain the different types of endosperms in angiosperms.
modelAnswer: The endosperm is the nutritive tissue formed in angiosperm seeds after triple fusion, and it is of three types based on the mode of endosperm development: 1. Nuclear endosperm: The primary endosperm nucleus divides repeatedly by free nuclear (mitotic) division without immediate wall formation, so numerous free nuclei are formed in a common cytoplasm; cell wall formation occurs later (centripetally), e.g. in coconut (the liquid coconut water represents free-nuclear endosperm stage). 2. Cellular endosperm: The primary endosperm nucleus divides and cell wall formation follows immediately after each nuclear division, so the endosperm is cellular right from the beginning, e.g. in Datura and Petunia. 3. Helobial endosperm: This is an intermediate type between nuclear and cellular endosperm, found in members of the Helobiales; the first division of the primary endosperm nucleus is followed by wall formation, dividing it into a large chalazal chamber and a smaller micropylar chamber, and subsequent divisions in each chamber may be nuclear or cellular.
keyPoints: Nuclear endosperm: repeated free-nuclear divisions before wall formation, e.g. coconut
Cellular endosperm: wall formation follows each nuclear division, e.g. Datura
Helobial endosperm: intermediate type, forms chalazal and micropylar chambers, e.g. Helobiales

subject: Biology
text: A homozygous pea plant with round seed coat and yellow cotyledons is crossed with another homozygous pea plant having wrinkled seed coat and green cotyledons. (i) Give the types of gametes produced by plants of the F1-generation. (ii) Give the dihybrid phenotypic ratio with the corresponding phenotypes. (iii) State the Mendel's principle involved in this cross.
modelAnswer: Parental cross: RRYY (round, yellow) x rryy (wrinkled, green). F1 generation: all RrYy (round, yellow - heterozygous for both traits). (i) F1 (RrYy) plants, during gamete formation, produce four types of gametes in equal proportion due to independent assortment of the two gene pairs: RY, Ry, rY and ry. (ii) On self-pollinating F1 (RrYy x RrYy), the F2 dihybrid phenotypic ratio obtained is 9:3:3:1 - 9 Round Yellow : 3 Round Green : 3 Wrinkled Yellow : 1 Wrinkled Green. (iii) This cross demonstrates Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, which states that when two pairs of contrasting traits (genes located on different chromosome pairs) are considered together in a cross, the alleles of one gene pair segregate/assort independently of the alleles of the other gene pair during gamete formation.
keyPoints: F1 = RrYy; produces 4 gamete types (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal ratio
F2 dihybrid ratio: 9 Round Yellow : 3 Round Green : 3 Wrinkled Yellow : 1 Wrinkled Green
Demonstrates Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment

subject: Biology
text: Describe the physico-chemical events that take place during fertilization in humans.
modelAnswer: Fertilization in humans occurs in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube and involves the following physico-chemical events: 1. Capacitation: As sperm travel through the female reproductive tract, they undergo functional/biochemical maturation (capacitation), which makes them capable of fertilizing the ovum. 2. Acrosomal reaction: On reaching the ovum, the capacitated sperm's acrosome releases hydrolytic/lytic enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase) upon contact with the corona radiata and zona pellucida of the secondary oocyte; these enzymes digest a path through these protective layers, allowing one sperm to penetrate. 3. Fusion of gametes: The plasma membrane of the sperm fuses with the plasma membrane of the oocyte, and the sperm nucleus enters the ooplasm. 4. Cortical reaction and zona reaction (block to polyspermy): Fusion triggers the release of cortical granules from the oocyte, which chemically alter the zona pellucida, making it impermeable to other sperm and thus preventing polyspermy (entry of more than one sperm). 5. Completion of meiosis: The secondary oocyte, which was arrested in metaphase II, resumes and completes meiosis II, forming the second polar body and a mature ovum (egg) nucleus. 6. Formation of zygote: The haploid male pronucleus and the haploid female pronucleus fuse (karyogamy) to restore the diploid number of chromosomes, forming a diploid zygote, which marks the completion of fertilization.
keyPoints: Capacitation of sperm in the female tract
Acrosomal reaction: enzymes digest corona radiata/zona pellucida
Sperm-oocyte membrane fusion; cortical reaction blocks polyspermy
Oocyte completes meiosis II; fusion of pronuclei (karyogamy) forms the diploid zygote

subject: Biology
text: [OR] (i) Define and give the role of amniocentesis. (ii) Name the causative agent and give any one symptom of Gonorrhoea. (iii) What is the significance of dispersal of seeds? Give any two points. (iv) What are seasonal breeders? Give an example. (v) How is the chromosome number maintained in sexually reproducing organisms?
modelAnswer: (i) Amniocentesis is a foetal sex-determination and prenatal diagnostic technique in which a sample of amniotic fluid (which contains foetal cells) is withdrawn and analysed for foetal chromosomal abnormalities and sex determination; it is legally banned for sex determination in India (under the PCPNDT Act) due to its misuse for female foeticide, but is used medically to detect genetic disorders. (ii) Gonorrhoea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae; a symptom is a painful/burning sensation during urination (or discharge from the genitals). (iii) Significance of seed dispersal: 1. It prevents overcrowding/competition between the parent plant and its offspring for light, water, and nutrients. 2. It allows the species to colonize and spread to new, distant habitats, reducing intraspecific competition and increasing chances of survival. (iv) Seasonal breeders are animals that breed/reproduce only during a specific favourable season of the year, becoming reproductively active only at that time; e.g. many wild animals like deer, and birds. (v) The chromosome number is maintained constant across generations in sexually reproducing organisms because meiosis (reductional division) during gamete formation halves the chromosome number (2n to n) in the gametes, and this haploid number is restored to the diploid (2n) state at fertilization when the male and female gametes fuse.
keyPoints: Amniocentesis: prenatal test of amniotic fluid for chromosomal defects/sex; banned for sex determination in India
Gonorrhoea caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae; symptom - painful urination
Seed dispersal prevents overcrowding and aids colonization of new habitats
Seasonal breeders reproduce only in a specific season, e.g. deer
Meiosis halves chromosome number in gametes; fertilization restores diploid number

subject: Biology
text: (i) What are restriction endonucleases? Give the rules of their nomenclature. (ii) Explain the mechanism of action of restriction endonucleases that makes them suitable for genetic engineering.
modelAnswer: (i) Restriction endonucleases are enzymes (a type of restriction enzyme) that recognize and cut/cleave double-stranded DNA at specific, short palindromic nucleotide sequences called recognition sequences. Nomenclature rules: The name is derived from the genus and species of the bacterium from which it was isolated - the first letter of the name comes from the genus, the next two letters from the species; this is followed by a letter/number indicating the strain, and a Roman numeral indicating the order of discovery/isolation from that organism (e.g. EcoRI: E from Escherichia, co from coli, R from strain RY13, I as the first enzyme isolated). (ii) Mechanism: Restriction endonucleases recognize a specific, usually palindromic, sequence of base pairs on the DNA (called the recognition site) and cut both strands of the DNA at or near this site, usually leaving 'sticky ends' (single-stranded overhangs with complementary bases) or blunt ends. This precise and predictable cutting ability makes them ideal molecular tools for genetic engineering - they can be used to cut out a desired gene from one DNA source and to cut open a vector (plasmid) at the same recognition site, so that the sticky ends of the gene and vector can base-pair and be joined together (using DNA ligase) to form recombinant DNA.
keyPoints: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences
Nomenclature: genus (1 letter) + species (2 letters) + strain + Roman numeral for order of discovery, e.g. EcoRI
Cutting produces sticky/blunt ends
Same enzyme cuts both gene-donor DNA and vector, enabling ligation into recombinant DNA

subject: Biology
text: [OR] (i) Explain what are the desirable characteristics of an ideal cloning vector used in rDNA technology. (ii) Describe two vectorless methods of gene transfer used in rDNA technology.
modelAnswer: (i) Desirable characteristics of an ideal cloning vector: 1. It should have an origin of replication (ori) that allows it to replicate independently and in high copy number within the host cell. 2. It should possess one or more selectable marker genes (e.g. antibiotic resistance genes) to help identify and select transformed host cells from non-transformed ones. 3. It should have a small number of, preferably unique, restriction sites (a multiple cloning site) so that a restriction enzyme can cut it at a single point for inserting foreign DNA without disrupting essential vector functions. 4. It should be small in size and easy to isolate/manipulate, for efficient uptake by the host cell. (ii) Vectorless methods of gene transfer: 1. Micro-injection: In this method, the desired/recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell (e.g. a fertilized egg) using a fine glass micropipette/needle. 2. Gene gun/Biolistics (particle bombardment): Here, DNA-coated microscopic gold or tungsten particles are physically shot/bombarded at high velocity directly into plant cells/tissues using a gene gun, and the DNA is delivered without using any vector.
keyPoints: Ideal vector needs: origin of replication, selectable marker gene, unique restriction sites, small size
Micro-injection: DNA directly injected into a cell/nucleus using a micropipette
Gene gun (biolistics): DNA-coated metal particles bombarded into cells at high velocity

subject: Biology
text: Give a graphic representation of the carbon cycle in nature and describe it.
modelAnswer: The carbon cycle describes the circulation of carbon through the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans and geological reservoirs. Atmospheric CO2 (about 0.03-0.04% of the atmosphere) is fixed by producers (green plants, algae, cyanobacteria) through photosynthesis into organic carbon compounds. This fixed carbon passes through the food chain from producers to herbivores to carnivores. Carbon is returned to the atmosphere as CO2 through respiration by all living organisms (plants, animals, decomposers), and through decomposition of dead organic matter by microbes. Additionally, combustion of fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient organisms) and forest fires/volcanic eruptions release large amounts of stored carbon back into the atmosphere as CO2. Oceans act as a huge reservoir of carbon, exchanging CO2 with the atmosphere and storing carbon as dissolved bicarbonates and in the shells/skeletons of marine organisms, some of which get deposited as limestone/fossil fuels over geological time. Diagrammatically: Atmospheric CO2 <-> [Photosynthesis by producers] -> Plants -> [Consumption] -> Herbivores -> Carnivores -> [Respiration/Decomposition] -> back to Atmospheric CO2; also Atmospheric CO2 <-> Oceans (dissolved carbon) <-> Sedimentation/Fossil fuels -> [Combustion] -> back to Atmospheric CO2.
keyPoints: Producers fix atmospheric CO2 via photosynthesis; carbon moves through food chain
Respiration and decomposition return carbon to the atmosphere as CO2
Combustion of fossil fuels and volcanic activity also release CO2
Oceans act as a major carbon reservoir (dissolved bicarbonate, marine shells/sediments)

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Give a graphic representation of the phosphorus cycle in nature and describe it.
modelAnswer: The phosphorus cycle is a sedimentary biogeochemical cycle (unlike the carbon and nitrogen cycles, it has no significant atmospheric/gaseous phase). The main reservoir of phosphorus is phosphate-containing rocks (e.g. apatite), which release phosphate ions into the soil and water through weathering and erosion. Plants absorb inorganic phosphate (as phosphate ions, PO4^3-) from the soil through their roots, and incorporate it into organic compounds (e.g. nucleic acids, ATP, phospholipids). This organic phosphorus passes along the food chain as herbivores consume plants and carnivores consume herbivores. Phosphorus is returned to the soil/environment when organisms excrete waste and when decomposers break down dead plant and animal matter, releasing inorganic phosphate back into the soil. A portion of phosphate is washed by rain/rivers into the ocean, where it may be taken up by marine organisms, or settle and become part of sedimentary rock on the ocean floor over long geological time periods, eventually being uplifted and weathered again, completing the slow cycle. Diagrammatically: Phosphate rocks -> [Weathering] -> Soil/Water phosphate -> [Absorption by plants] -> Plants -> [Consumption] -> Animals -> [Excretion/Decomposition] -> back to Soil phosphate; also Soil/River phosphate -> Ocean -> Sedimentation -> Rocks (geological uplift closes the cycle).
keyPoints: Phosphorus cycle is sedimentary - main reservoir is rock, no major atmospheric phase
Weathering of rocks releases phosphate into soil/water, absorbed by plant roots
Phosphorus passes through food chain; decomposition returns it to soil
Runoff carries phosphate to oceans, where it sediments into rock over geological time

subject: Biology
text: Why is haemophilia uncommon in females?
modelAnswer: Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder. For a female to be haemophilic, she must inherit the recessive allele on both her X chromosomes (be homozygous recessive, X^h X^h), which requires her father to be haemophilic and mother to be at least a carrier - a rare combination. In contrast, a male needs only one recessive allele on his single X chromosome to be haemophilic. Hence, haemophilia is much less common in females than in males.
keyPoints: X-linked recessive disorder
Females need two copies (homozygous recessive) to be affected - a rarer combination
Males need only one recessive allele (hemizygous), so it is more common in males

subject: Biology
text: Define polygenic inheritance.
modelAnswer: Polygenic inheritance is a pattern of inheritance in which a single phenotypic trait (e.g. human skin colour, height) is controlled by the cumulative, additive effect of multiple genes (each with a small individual effect) located at different loci, often also influenced by the environment, resulting in a continuous range of phenotypic variation.
keyPoints: A single trait is controlled by multiple genes with additive effects
Produces continuous variation, e.g. human skin colour, height

subject: Biology
text: What is Dobson unit?
modelAnswer: The Dobson Unit (DU) is the unit used to measure and express the total amount/concentration of ozone present in a vertical column of the Earth's atmosphere (stratospheric ozone layer thickness).

subject: Biology
text: Define: Aneuploidy.
modelAnswer: Aneuploidy is a chromosomal abnormality in which an organism has one or more chromosomes added to or missing from its normal diploid chromosome number (i.e. the chromosome number is not an exact multiple of the haploid number), e.g. trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome) with 2n+1 = 47 chromosomes.
keyPoints: Aneuploidy = abnormal chromosome number due to addition/loss of individual chromosomes
E.g. Down's syndrome (trisomy 21): 2n+1 = 47 chromosomes

subject: Biology
text: Give a reason: Cyanobacteria increase the productivity in paddy fields.
modelAnswer: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae, e.g. Anabaena, Nostoc) are free-living nitrogen-fixing organisms that convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogenous compounds (biological nitrogen fixation) in the waterlogged soil of paddy fields, thereby naturally enriching the soil with nitrogen (a limiting nutrient) and increasing the productivity/yield of the paddy crop without the need for chemical fertilizers.
keyPoints: Cyanobacteria (e.g. Anabaena, Nostoc) fix atmospheric nitrogen
Enrich paddy field soil with nitrogen, boosting crop productivity naturally

subject: Biology
text: Give a reason: The shape of the pyramid of biomass in an aquatic ecosystem is inverted.
modelAnswer: In an aquatic (pond) ecosystem, the biomass of producers (phytoplankton) at any given time is very small because they are microscopic, have a short life span and reproduce/turn over very rapidly, being continuously and quickly consumed by a much larger standing biomass of zooplankton and fish (consumers). Hence, the biomass increases progressively from lower to higher trophic levels, giving the pyramid of biomass an inverted (upright-down) shape.
keyPoints: Producers (phytoplankton) have small standing biomass at any instant due to rapid turnover
Consumer biomass (zooplankton, fish) exceeds producer biomass, inverting the pyramid shape

subject: Biology
text: Give one significant difference between the following: (i) Linkage and crossing over (ii) Transition and transversion.
modelAnswer: (i) Linkage is the tendency of genes located close together on the same chromosome to be inherited together (as a unit) rather than independently, whereas crossing over is the actual physical process/event of exchange of segments/genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiosis (prophase I), which breaks linkage and produces new gene combinations (recombinants). (ii) A transition is a point mutation in which a purine base is substituted by another purine (A <-> G) or a pyrimidine by another pyrimidine (C <-> T), whereas a transversion is a point mutation in which a purine is substituted by a pyrimidine or vice versa (e.g. A <-> C, or G <-> T).
keyPoints: Linkage: genes on same chromosome tend to be inherited together; crossing over: physical exchange of segments between homologous chromatids that breaks linkage
Transition: purine<->purine or pyrimidine<->pyrimidine substitution; transversion: purine<->pyrimidine substitution

subject: Biology
text: What is biogas? Name any two main constituents of biogas.
modelAnswer: Biogas is a combustible/flammable gaseous fuel produced by the anaerobic (in the absence of oxygen) microbial decomposition/fermentation of organic matter (such as animal dung, agricultural waste, and other biodegradable material) inside a biogas plant/digester by methanogenic bacteria. Two main constituents of biogas are methane (CH4, the main combustible component, about 50-70%) and carbon dioxide (CO2); it also contains small amounts of hydrogen sulphide and other gases.
keyPoints: Biogas = flammable gas from anaerobic microbial decomposition of organic waste
Main constituents: methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2)

subject: Biology
text: Explain two characteristics of cancer cells.
modelAnswer: 1. Loss of contact inhibition: Unlike normal cells, cancer cells do not stop dividing when they come into contact with neighbouring cells; they continue to divide uncontrollably, piling up to form a mass/tumour. 2. Invasiveness and metastasis: Cancer cells have the ability to invade the surrounding normal tissue and can spread/migrate through blood or lymph to distant parts of the body, establishing secondary tumours (metastasis) - a property that normal cells lack.
keyPoints: Loss of contact inhibition - cells divide uncontrollably even in contact with neighbours
Invasive and metastatic - able to spread to distant body parts via blood/lymph

subject: Biology
text: What is outbreeding? How is it useful in animal breeding?
modelAnswer: Outbreeding is the mating/breeding of unrelated animals (belonging to the same breed but having no common ancestors for 4-6 generations, or between different breeds/species), as opposed to inbreeding (mating of closely related individuals). Usefulness in animal breeding: Outbreeding helps avoid the harmful effects of inbreeding depression (reduced fertility and productivity), and it introduces new, favourable genetic variation/hybrid vigour (heterosis) into the population, leading to healthier, more productive and disease-resistant offspring; it is used in practices such as outcrossing, cross-breeding and interspecific hybridization.
keyPoints: Outbreeding = mating of unrelated animals (no common ancestors for several generations)
Avoids inbreeding depression and introduces hybrid vigour (heterosis), improving productivity and health

subject: Biology
text: (a) What is biomagnification? Write two effects of biomagnification. [OR] (b) Write a short note on the contribution of Ahmed Khan of Bangalore.
modelAnswer: (a) Biomagnification is the process by which the concentration of certain non-biodegradable toxic substances (such as pesticides like DDT, heavy metals) progressively increases in the tissues of organisms at each successive trophic level of a food chain, being highest in the top carnivores. Effects: 1. It causes serious, often fatal, health effects (e.g. reproductive/nervous system damage, thinning of egg shells in birds) in top carnivores that accumulate the highest concentrations. 2. It disrupts food chains and reduces biodiversity, and toxic substances can eventually also affect/poison humans, who often occupy a high trophic level.
keyPoints: Biomagnification = increasing concentration of toxins (e.g. DDT) at successive trophic levels
Effects: severe harm to top carnivores (e.g. eggshell thinning in birds); disrupts food chains and can affect human health

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Write a short note on the contribution of Ahmed Khan of Bangalore.
modelAnswer: Ahmed Khan of Bangalore is credited with developing an innovative technology (in association with the KK Plastic Waste Management Ltd.) to recycle waste plastic by shredding it and mixing it with bitumen for use in the construction/laying of roads. This method (called 'polymer/plastic composite roads' or 'polymerized bitumen roads') provides a practical and economical solution for disposing of non-biodegradable plastic waste, reducing plastic pollution, while also creating more durable roads.
keyPoints: Ahmed Khan pioneered using shredded waste plastic mixed with bitumen for road construction
Provides an eco-friendly solution to plastic waste disposal while producing more durable roads

subject: Biology
text: Give three adaptations in organisms by which they avoid predation.
modelAnswer: 1. Cryptic colouration (camouflage): Many organisms have body colouration that blends with their surroundings, making them difficult for predators to detect, e.g. stick insects, frogs. 2. Warning colouration (aposematism): Some organisms that are toxic or unpalatable have bright, conspicuous colouration to warn/signal potential predators to avoid them, e.g. the Monarch butterfly. 3. Mimicry: A palatable/harmless species may closely resemble an unpalatable/toxic or dangerous species in appearance to deter predators, e.g. the Viceroy butterfly mimicking the toxic Monarch butterfly.
keyPoints: Cryptic colouration/camouflage - blends with surroundings
Warning colouration/aposematism - signals toxicity to predators
Mimicry - palatable species resembles a toxic/dangerous one to avoid predation

subject: Biology
text: (a) Define decomposition. Explain main steps involved in the process of decomposition. [OR] (b) Write three causes and three effects of cultural eutrophication.
modelAnswer: (a) Decomposition is the process by which decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down complex organic matter present in dead plant and animal remains (detritus) into simpler inorganic substances. Main steps: 1. Fragmentation: Detritivores (e.g. earthworms) break down detritus into smaller particles. 2. Leaching: Water-soluble inorganic nutrients present in the detritus percolate/dissolve down into the soil and get precipitated as unavailable salts. 3. Catabolism: Decomposer enzymes (bacterial/fungal) degrade the fragmented detritus into simpler inorganic substances through enzymatic breakdown. 4. Humification: This leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes very slowly. 5. Mineralization: Humus is further degraded by some microorganisms, releasing inorganic nutrients (minerals) back into the soil, which can be reabsorbed by plant roots.
keyPoints: Decomposition = breakdown of dead organic matter by decomposers into simpler inorganic substances
Steps: fragmentation -> leaching -> catabolism -> humification -> mineralization

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Write three causes and three effects of cultural eutrophication.
modelAnswer: Causes: 1. Runoff of excess chemical fertilizers (nitrates, phosphates) from agricultural fields into water bodies. 2. Discharge of untreated or partially treated domestic sewage and industrial effluents into lakes/rivers. 3. Discharge of detergents and other nutrient-rich waste materials into water bodies. Effects: 1. Excessive/algal bloom growth on the water surface, blocking sunlight penetration to deeper layers. 2. Depletion of dissolved oxygen in water (as decomposers consuming dead algae use up oxygen), leading to death of fish and other aquatic organisms. 3. Loss of biodiversity and deterioration of water quality, making it unfit for drinking or other uses.
keyPoints: Causes: fertilizer runoff, sewage discharge, detergent/industrial effluent discharge
Effects: algal bloom blocking sunlight, oxygen depletion causing fish kills, loss of aquatic biodiversity and water quality

subject: Biology
text: (i) Write two differences between homologous organs and analogous organs. (ii) Give one example of homologous organs and one example of analogous organs found in plants.
modelAnswer: (i) Homologous organs have a similar/common basic structure and developmental origin, but may perform different functions in different organisms, and their similarity arises due to divergent evolution from a common ancestor. Analogous organs, on the other hand, have different basic structure/origin but perform a similar function, and their similarity arises due to convergent evolution (adapting to similar environments/needs independently), not from a common ancestor. (ii) Example of homologous organs in plants: The thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita (both are modified stems, similar origin, different functions - defence vs climbing). Example of analogous organs in plants: The thorn of Bougainvillea (modified stem) and the spine of Opuntia/cactus (modified leaf) - both perform the same function (defence) but have different origins.
keyPoints: Homologous organs: same origin/structure, different function - divergent evolution
Analogous organs: different origin, similar function - convergent evolution
Plant example (homologous): thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita (both modified stems)
Plant example (analogous): thorn of Bougainvillea (modified stem) and spine of Opuntia (modified leaf)

subject: Biology
text: Describe the process of double fertilization in angiosperms. What is its significance?
modelAnswer: Double fertilization is a unique phenomenon in angiosperms in which two fusion events occur inside the embryo sac. When the pollen tube reaches the embryo sac (after entering through the micropyle, typically via porogamy), it releases two male gametes into the cytoplasm of the synergid. 1. Syngamy: One of the two male gametes (n) fuses with the egg cell (n) to form a diploid (2n) zygote, which later develops into the embryo. 2. Triple fusion: The second male gamete (n) fuses with the two polar nuclei (or the secondary/diploid central cell nucleus formed by their fusion) located in the central cell, resulting in the formation of a triploid (3n) Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN). Since this process of fertilization involves two distinct fusion events (syngamy and triple fusion) within the same embryo sac, it is termed 'double fertilization'. Significance: The zygote (from syngamy) develops into the embryo (the new sporophyte), while the Primary Endosperm Nucleus (from triple fusion) develops into the endosperm, a nutritive tissue that provides nourishment to the developing embryo; this ensures that nutritive tissue is formed only when fertilization has actually occurred, avoiding wastage of resources.
keyPoints: Two male gametes released by pollen tube into the embryo sac
Syngamy: male gamete + egg cell -> diploid zygote (develops into embryo)
Triple fusion: second male gamete + 2 polar nuclei -> triploid PEN (develops into endosperm)
Significance: endosperm formed only after fertilization, nourishing the embryo - avoids resource wastage

subject: Biology
text: What is a bioreactor? Explain important features of a Stirred tank bioreactor.
modelAnswer: A bioreactor is a large vessel/container used for the large-scale (industrial) production of biotechnological/biological products from raw materials, using living cells/microorganisms or their enzymes under optimum, controlled growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, oxygen, etc.). Features of a Stirred-tank bioreactor: 1. It has a cylindrical vessel with a curved base to facilitate mixing of the reactor contents. 2. It is fitted with a stirrer (agitator system) that mixes the contents uniformly, ensuring even distribution of nutrients, oxygen and cells throughout the vessel. 3. The stirrer also helps in maintaining uniform aeration (oxygen availability) throughout the bioreactor. 4. An outlet is provided to draw off/withdraw a portion of the product/culture at intervals. 5. The vessel typically has a foam breaker to control excessive foam formation, and ports for temperature and pH probes to monitor and control the culture conditions.
keyPoints: Bioreactor = vessel for large-scale production using living cells/enzymes under controlled conditions
Stirred-tank bioreactor: cylindrical with curved base and a stirrer/agitator for uniform mixing and aeration
Has ports for monitoring temperature/pH and an outlet to withdraw product

subject: Biology
text: Give three significant differences between asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction.
modelAnswer: 1. Asexual reproduction involves only a single parent, whereas sexual reproduction requires two parents (or gametes from two parents, though some organisms may be self-fertilizing). 2. Asexual reproduction does not involve the formation or fusion of gametes, whereas sexual reproduction involves the formation of haploid gametes (by meiosis) and their fusion (fertilization) to form a zygote. 3. Offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical (clones) to the parent, showing little/no variation, whereas offspring produced by sexual reproduction show genetic variation due to recombination and independent assortment during meiosis, making them genetically different from both parents.
keyPoints: Asexual: single parent; Sexual: two parents/gametes involved
Asexual: no gamete formation/fusion; Sexual: involves meiosis, gamete formation and fertilization
Asexual: offspring are genetically identical clones; Sexual: offspring show genetic variation

subject: Biology
text: (a) Explain the process of spermatogenesis in humans. [OR] (b) Give an account of hormonal control of oogenesis.
modelAnswer: (a) Spermatogenesis is the process of formation of male gametes (sperm) that occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, starting at puberty. It involves: 1. Spermatocytogenesis: Diploid spermatogonial (germinal) cells lining the seminiferous tubules multiply by mitosis to increase in number; some differentiate into primary spermatocytes (2n). 2. Meiosis: Each primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I to form two haploid secondary spermatocytes (n), which then undergo meiosis II to form four haploid spermatids (n) in total. 3. Spermiogenesis: The spermatids undergo a process of transformation/differentiation (spermiogenesis) into mature, motile spermatozoa, characterized by the development of a head, midpiece with mitochondria, and a flagellum/tail. 4. Spermiation: The mature sperm are then released from the Sertoli cells into the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. This whole process is regulated by hormones - GnRH from the hypothalamus stimulates the pituitary to release LH and FSH; LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, and FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis.
keyPoints: Spermatogonia (2n) multiply by mitosis, form primary spermatocytes
Meiosis I & II convert primary spermatocyte into 4 haploid spermatids
Spermiogenesis: spermatids differentiate into motile spermatozoa
Regulated by GnRH -> LH (stimulates Leydig cells - testosterone) and FSH (acts on Sertoli cells)

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Give an account of hormonal control of oogenesis.
modelAnswer: Oogenesis (formation of the female gamete/ovum) and the associated menstrual cycle are regulated by a complex interplay of hormones. The hypothalamus secretes GnRH (Gonadotropin Releasing Hormone), which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete two gonadotropins - FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) and LH (Luteinizing Hormone). FSH stimulates the growth and maturation of ovarian (Graafian) follicles, and along with LH, stimulates the follicular cells to secrete oestrogen, which causes proliferation of the uterine endometrium. A surge in LH (the LH surge) at around the mid-cycle stage induces rupture of the mature Graafian follicle, causing ovulation (release of the secondary oocyte). After ovulation, LH also stimulates transformation of the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone; progesterone maintains/prepares the endometrium for implantation. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, hormone levels (oestrogen and progesterone) fall, and the endometrium is shed as menstruation, restarting the cycle.
keyPoints: GnRH from hypothalamus stimulates pituitary to release FSH and LH
FSH matures Graafian follicles; oestrogen from follicle causes endometrial proliferation
LH surge triggers ovulation; LH converts ruptured follicle to corpus luteum
Corpus luteum secretes progesterone, maintaining endometrium for implantation; its degeneration (if no fertilization) causes menstruation

subject: Biology
text: Explain the various steps involved in Recombinant DNA technology.
modelAnswer: Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology involves the following main steps: 1. Isolation of genetic material (DNA): DNA is extracted and purified from the source cell, free of other macromolecules like RNA and proteins. 2. Cutting of DNA (using restriction enzymes): The desired gene (from the donor) and a vector (e.g. plasmid) are both cut using the same specific restriction endonuclease, producing complementary 'sticky ends'. 3. Ligation (joining of DNA fragments): The cut gene of interest is inserted/joined into the cut vector using the enzyme DNA ligase, forming a recombinant DNA molecule. 4. Insertion of recombinant DNA into the host cell: The recombinant DNA (vector + insert) is introduced into a suitable host cell (bacterium, yeast, plant or animal cell) through a process called transformation (e.g. using calcium chloride treatment and heat shock to make bacterial cells competent). 5. Selection of transformed host cells: Transformed cells (those that have taken up the recombinant DNA) are selected/identified from non-transformed cells using selectable marker genes present on the vector (e.g. antibiotic resistance genes, or blue-white selection). 6. Multiplication/expression of the foreign gene in the host: The selected transformed host cells are cultured/grown under optimum conditions (often in a bioreactor) so that they multiply, expressing the foreign gene and producing the desired protein/product on a large scale. 7. Downstream processing: The desired product is then extracted, purified and formulated/processed appropriately for commercial use.
keyPoints: Isolation of DNA -> cutting with restriction enzymes (gene of interest + vector)
Ligation of gene into vector using DNA ligase forms recombinant DNA
Transformation - recombinant DNA introduced into host cell
Selection of transformants using marker genes; culturing (bioreactor) for large-scale expression; downstream processing

subject: Biology
text: [OR] Explain the steps involved in the production of human insulin by Recombinant DNA technology.
modelAnswer: Human insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, the A chain (21 amino acids) and the B chain (30 amino acids), linked together by disulfide bonds. Production using rDNA technology (by the company Eli Lilly, product Humulin): 1. Two separate synthetic DNA sequences corresponding to the A chain and B chain of human insulin were prepared and separately inserted into two different plasmid vectors, each next to the lacZ gene sequence, in E. coli. 2. Each type of transformed E. coli cell culture was grown separately, and each produced its respective insulin chain (A or B) as a fusion protein attached to the beta-galactosidase enzyme (a marker of successful expression). 3. The two chains (A and B) were extracted and purified separately, then treated to cleave the insulin chains from the beta-galactosidase using appropriate chemical/enzymatic treatment. 4. The purified A and B chains were then combined and joined together in vitro through the formation of disulfide bonds, to reconstitute the complete, biologically active, functional human insulin molecule, which was then purified and packaged for use in treating diabetes.
keyPoints: Insulin has A chain (21 aa) and B chain (30 aa) joined by disulfide bonds
Two DNA sequences (A and B chains) separately cloned and expressed in E. coli (Eli Lilly's Humulin)
Chains extracted, purified and treated to separate from beta-galactosidase fusion
A and B chains combined in vitro via disulfide bonds to form active insulin

subject: Biology
text: (i) Give an account of Meselson and Stahl's experiment. (ii) What is the significance of Meselson and Stahl's experiment?
modelAnswer: (i) Meselson and Stahl's experiment (1958) was designed to prove that DNA replication is semi-conservative. They grew E. coli bacteria for several generations in a medium containing the heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N) as the only nitrogen source, so that all the bacterial DNA became labelled with heavy nitrogen (15N-15N, heavy DNA). They then transferred these bacteria to a medium containing only the normal, light isotope of nitrogen (14N) and allowed the bacteria to divide, extracting and analysing DNA after each generation using density gradient centrifugation (in a caesium chloride, CsCl, gradient), which separates DNA molecules based on their density/molecular weight. Results: After one generation (one round of replication) in the 14N medium, all the DNA extracted was found to be of an intermediate/hybrid density (between pure heavy 15N-15N DNA and pure light 14N-14N DNA), indicating that each DNA molecule now contained one heavy (15N) strand and one light (14N) strand. After a second generation, two types of DNA were found in equal proportions - hybrid (intermediate) density DNA and light (14N-14N) density DNA, but no fully heavy DNA was found. (ii) Significance: These results, matching Watson and Crick's prediction, provided direct experimental proof that DNA replicates semi-conservatively - i.e. each daughter DNA molecule retains (conserves) one original (parental) strand and synthesizes one new complementary strand, ruling out the alternative conservative and dispersive models of replication.
keyPoints: Grew E. coli in 15N (heavy) medium, then shifted to 14N (light) medium
Used CsCl density gradient centrifugation to separate DNA by density
Gen 1: all DNA hybrid (intermediate) density; Gen 2: half hybrid, half light density, no fully heavy DNA
Proved DNA replication is semi-conservative (each daughter molecule has one old + one new strand)

subject: Biology
text: [OR] (i) Describe the Oparin Haldane Theory of origin of life. (ii) The tadpole larva of amphibians resembles fishes. How does this observation support evolution?
modelAnswer: (i) The Oparin-Haldane theory (chemical evolution theory), proposed independently by A.I. Oparin and J.B.S. Haldane, states that life on Earth originated from non-living (inorganic/simple organic) matter through a slow and gradual process of chemical evolution. According to this theory, the primitive Earth's atmosphere was reducing in nature, consisting of gases such as methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3), hydrogen (H2) and water vapour, but lacking free oxygen. Under the influence of energy sources such as UV radiation from the sun, lightning, and volcanic heat, these simple inorganic molecules combined to form simple organic compounds (like amino acids and simple sugars). These simple organic molecules further combined and became progressively more complex, forming macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids), which then aggregated to form colloidal complexes called coacervates, which were surrounded by a membrane-like boundary and could grow, divide, and carry out crude metabolic reactions - these coacervates further evolved through natural selection over long periods into the first primitive, simple living cells (protobionts), leading eventually to the first true living cells. (ii) The tadpole larva of frogs (amphibians) has gills and a fish-like tail, resembling the larval/adult stage of fish, before it metamorphoses into the adult frog with lungs and no gills. This resemblance of an early developmental stage of amphibians to the fish reflects their evolutionary ancestry - amphibians are believed to have evolved from a fish-like ancestor, and this observation reflects the principle that 'ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny' (the idea that stages in the embryonic/larval development of an organism often mirror the evolutionary stages/history of its ancestors), thus providing evidence in support of the theory of evolution.
keyPoints: Oparin-Haldane theory: life arose from non-living matter via chemical evolution in a reducing early atmosphere
Simple gases (CH4, NH3, H2, H2O) formed organic molecules under UV/lightning/heat; evolved into coacervates and then primitive cells
Tadpole resembling fish reflects amphibians' evolutionary origin from fish-like ancestors
Illustrates that development (ontogeny) can reflect evolutionary history (phylogeny) - evidence for evolution

subject: Biology
text: Name any two Cu-ion releasing IUDs. Explain any two ways by which these devices act as contraceptives.
modelAnswer:
Two Cu-ion releasing IUDs: (1) CuT (Copper T) (2) Cu7 (Copper 7) / Multiload 375

Two ways they act as contraceptives:
(i) Cu²⁺ ions released are toxic to sperms — they reduce sperm motility and suppress their fertilising capacity, preventing fertilisation.
(ii) They make the uterine environment unfavourable for implantation by causing changes in the uterine wall (endometrium), preventing implantation of the blastocyst even if fertilisation occurs.
keyPoints: CuT and Cu7/Multiload 375 are Cu-ion IUDs
Mechanism 1: Cu ions are toxic/spermicidal — reduce sperm motility; Mechanism 2: make uterine environment hostile to implantation

subject: Biology
text: A population of 200 fruit flies is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The frequency of allele (a) is 0.4. Calculate: (i) Frequency of allele (A), (ii) Number of homozygous dominant fruit flies, (iii) Number of homozygous recessive fruit flies, (iv) Number of carrier fruit flies.
modelAnswer:
Given: q = 0.4 (frequency of a), total population N = 200

(i) Frequency of A: p = 1 − q = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6

(ii) Homozygous dominant (AA): p² × N = (0.6)² × 200 = 0.36 × 200 = 72 flies

(iii) Homozygous recessive (aa): q² × N = (0.4)² × 200 = 0.16 × 200 = 32 flies

(iv) Carrier (Aa) (heterozygous): 2pq × N = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 200 = 0.48 × 200 = 96 flies
keyPoints: p = 0.6; AA = 72; aa = 32; Aa (carriers) = 96
Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1; genotype frequencies p², 2pq, q²

text: Jacob is genetically a carrier of the disorder that affects the shape of the RBCs (sickle-shaped cells). His son James suffers from the same disorder. (i) Give the biochemical reason for the disorder that changes the shape of the RBCs. (ii) Draw a Punnett square to show the genotype of the mother of James. (iii) Name and define the type of 'point mutation' responsible for this disorder.

(ii) Jacob (carrier) = HbA HbS; Mother of James must also be a carrier (HbA HbS) since James (HbS HbS) inherited HbS from both parents:

HbA: HbAHbA  HbAHbS
HbS: HbAHbS  HbSHbS
James (HbS HbS) can only arise if mother is also HbA HbS (carrier).

(iii) Type of point mutation: Missense mutation — a single nucleotide substitution (GAG → GUG / CTC → CAC at DNA level) that changes the codon so that a different amino acid (valine instead of glutamic acid) is incorporated into the protein.
keyPoints: Glutamic acid → Valine substitution in β-globin; HbS polymerises in low O₂ causing sickle shape
Mother must be carrier (HbA HbS); Missense mutation (single base substitution changes amino acid)

text: The diagram shows three types of endosperms in angiosperms (Type 1: free nuclei/Nuclear, Type 2: Cellular, Type 3: Helobial). (a) Identify the three types of endosperms. (b) Name the type of endosperm which commonly occurs in polypetalous dicots.

text: A male plant bearing red flowers was crossed with a female plant bearing yellow flowers. In the F₁ generation, all the flowers were orange in colour. (i) Give a reason to explain the change of colours in F₁ generation. (ii) Mention the ratio of red flowers, yellow flowers and orange flowers in the F₂ generation.

• Phenotype: 1 Red : 2 Orange : 1 Yellow

text: The diagram shows L.S. of a typical fruit with parts labelled 1, 2, 3. (i) Identify the parts labelled 1, 2 and 3. (ii) State the difference between a true fruit and a false fruit. (iii) What is the significance of formation of fruit in angiosperms?
modelAnswer:
(i) In a typical fruit (e.g., mango):
• Part 1 → Epicarp (outer skin/pericarp)
• Part 2 → Mesocarp (fleshy middle part/pericarp)
• Part 3 → Endocarp (innermost hard layer/pericarp surrounding the seed)

(ii) True fruit vs False fruit:
• True fruit: develops entirely from the fertilised ovary of the flower (e.g., mango, grape)
• False fruit (pseudocarp): develops from the thalamus or other floral parts in addition to or instead of the ovary (e.g., apple, strawberry — mainly from thalamus)

(iii) Significance of fruit formation:
• Protects the developing seeds from desiccation and mechanical injury.
• Helps in seed dispersal — fleshy fruits attract animals that consume them and disperse seeds; dry fruits have adaptations (wings, hooks) for wind/water/animal dispersal.
• Provides nourishment to the embryo/seed during development.

Significance: seed protection and dispersal

subject: Biology
text: Suneeta is planning to clone a gene in a vector. Three vectors A, B, C are shown (Vector A has lacZ, ori, rop, multiple restriction sites; Vector B has ori, rop, multiple sites but no selectable marker visible; Vector C has ampR, tetR, ori, rop, multiple restriction sites). Which one should she choose? Justify with two reasons.
modelAnswer:
Suneeta should choose Vector C.

Justification (two reasons):
1. Vector C has two selectable antibiotic resistance markers (ampR — ampicillin resistance, and tetR — tetracycline resistance). This enables insertional inactivation — when a foreign gene is inserted into the tetR gene, tetracycline resistance is disrupted, allowing easy identification of recombinant clones (colonies grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline = recombinants).

2. Vector C has multiple cloning sites (MCS) with different restriction enzyme recognition sites (EcoRI, ClaI, HindIII, BamHI, PvuI, PstI) at multiple positions, including within both marker genes. This gives greater flexibility in choosing the appropriate restriction enzyme for cloning without losing both markers.
keyPoints: Choose Vector C: has two antibiotic resistance markers (ampR, tetR) enabling insertional inactivation
Multiple restriction sites in the tetR gene allow insertional inactivation for easy recombinant identification

subject: Biology
text: Two growth model figures are shown: Figure A (J-shaped/exponential) and Figure B (S-shaped/logistic). (i) Which figure represents unlimited supply of nutrients? Give a reason. (ii) Which figure depicts a challenge to population growth? (iii) Explain the term reproductive fitness. (iv) Give the mathematical expressions for Figure A and Figure B.
modelAnswer:
(i) Figure A (J-shaped/exponential curve) represents unlimited supply of nutrients. The population grows at an ever-increasing rate because there are no limiting factors — food, space and other resources are assumed to be unlimited, so each individual can reproduce without competition.

(ii) Figure B (S-shaped/logistic curve) depicts a challenge to population growth. As the population approaches the carrying capacity (K), intraspecific competition for limited resources intensifies, slowing growth and creating a challenge.

(iii) Reproductive fitness: The relative ability of an individual (or genotype) to survive to reproductive age and produce viable offspring in a given environment, contributing its genes to the next generation. It is a measure of how well an organism's traits are adapted to its environment.

(iv) Mathematical expressions:
• Figure A (Exponential growth): dN/dt = rN (where r = intrinsic rate of natural increase, N = population size)
• Figure B (Logistic growth): dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K (where K = carrying capacity)
keyPoints: Fig A (J-shaped): unlimited nutrients, dN/dt = rN
Fig B (S-shaped): limited resources/carrying capacity K, dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K
Reproductive fitness: ability to survive and produce viable offspring

subject: Biology
text: The diagram shows the schematic structure of proinsulin (A chain, B chain, C-peptide). (i) State the change proinsulin undergoes to become fully functional. (ii) Name the modern scientific technique used for the production of human insulin. (iii) How are the two polypeptide chains of fully functional insulin held together?
modelAnswer:
(i) To become fully functional insulin, the C-peptide (connecting peptide) is enzymatically cleaved/removed from proinsulin. This leaves the A-chain and B-chain, which form the mature, active insulin molecule.

(ii) Recombinant DNA technology (rDNA technology / Genetic engineering) is used. The human insulin gene is cloned into a bacterial vector (E. coli) — the A and B chains are produced separately and then combined to form functional insulin (Humulin).

(iii) The A-chain and B-chain of mature insulin are held together by two disulphide bonds (S–S bonds) formed between cysteine residues in the two chains. Additionally, there is one intra-chain disulphide bond within the A-chain.
keyPoints: C-peptide removed from proinsulin to form active insulin
Recombinant DNA technology (rDNA); insulin gene expressed in E. coli
Two polypeptide chains held by disulphide bonds (between cysteine residues)

subject: Biology
text: A patient was given an anti-retroviral drug by the doctor. (i) Which disease was the patient diagnosed with? Mention any one symptom. (ii) Give the scientific name of the causative agent. (iii) Which method was used to diagnose this disease? (iv) What is the role of Reverse Transcriptase and Integrase in the life cycle of a retrovirus?
modelAnswer:
(i) The patient was diagnosed with AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome). One symptom: persistent fever, weight loss, night sweats, recurrent infections, or swollen lymph nodes (any one).

(ii) Causative agent: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) — scientific name: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) / Lentivirus.

(iii) Diagnosis method: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) — detects HIV antibodies in blood. Confirmed by Western Blot test or PCR.

(iv) Roles in retrovirus life cycle:
• Reverse Transcriptase: Transcribes viral single-stranded RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA), then synthesises the second DNA strand to form double-stranded viral DNA (converts RNA → DNA, reverse of normal transcription).
• Integrase: Integrates the viral double-stranded DNA into the host cell's chromosome as a provirus, allowing it to be replicated along with the host genome.
keyPoints: AIDS; diagnosed by ELISA/Western Blot
Causative agent: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus)
Reverse transcriptase: RNA→DNA; Integrase: inserts viral DNA into host chromosome
