text: The table shows Area (A), Y-intercept (C), and regression coefficient (Z) for Africa (A=62,000 km², C=10, Z=1) and Europe (A=65,000 km², C=20, Z=1). Using the species-area relationship log S = log C + Z log A: (i) Calculate the species richness (S) of each continent. (ii) Which shows higher biodiversity? (iii) State any two factors that cause an increase in biodiversity.
modelAnswer:
(i) Species-area relationship: log S = log C + Z log A

Africa: log S = log(10) + 1 × log(62,000)
= 1 + log(62,000) = 1 + 4.7924 = 5.7924
S_Africa ≈ 10^5.7924 ≈ 619,785 species

Europe: log S = log(20) + 1 × log(65,000)
= 1.3010 + 4.8129 = 6.1139
S_Europe ≈ 10^6.1139 ≈ 1,299,760 species

(ii) Europe shows higher biodiversity (S_Europe > S_Africa), despite slightly larger area, mainly due to the higher Y-intercept (C = 20 vs 10), which reflects a higher base species density.

(iii) Two factors that increase biodiversity:
1. Larger area — larger geographic area supports more species (species-area relationship)
2. Greater habitat diversity / variety of microhabitats — diverse ecosystems support more species (e.g., tropical rainforests)
(Also: warmer climate / lower latitude; higher primary productivity)
keyPoints: Africa S ≈ 619,785; Europe S ≈ 1,299,760; Europe has higher biodiversity
Factors: larger area, habitat diversity (also warmer climate, greater productivity)

subject: Biology
text: Meena collected pollen from China-rose plants and placed them on the stigma of Rose flowers to grow a hybrid. (a) Will this pollination give the desired results? Give a reason. (b) What is geitonogamy? Why is it considered equivalent to cross-pollination in ecological context and self-pollination in genetic context?
modelAnswer:
(a) No, this pollination will NOT give the desired results. The reason is that China-rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) and Rose (Rosa sp.) belong to different species (and different genera), though both are in the family Malvaceae and Rosaceae respectively. Interspecific pollination between different species (even the same family) generally does not result in successful fertilisation because of genetic incompatibility — the pollen tube cannot grow or fertilise the egg cell due to species-specific recognition barriers.

(b) Geitonogamy: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower on the same plant. (Different flowers of the same individual plant.)

• Equivalent to cross-pollination ecologically: It involves a pollinating agent (insects, wind, etc.) that physically carries pollen from one flower to another, just like in cross-pollination. In ecological terms, the mechanism of pollination is the same.

• Equivalent to self-pollination genetically: Since both flowers are on the same plant, they have identical (or nearly identical) genetic makeup. No new genetic combinations are introduced, so genetically the outcome is the same as self-pollination — no genetic variation or outbreeding benefit.
keyPoints: No — different species (incompatibility); Geitonogamy = pollen transfer between flowers of same plant
Ecological cross-pollination: uses a pollinator/agent; Genetic self-pollination: same genotype, no new variation

subject: Biology
text: The diagram shows decomposition in a forest ecosystem with falling leaves, earthworms, and centipedes. (i) Why is breaking down of complex organic matter an important event in the ecosystem? (ii) The forest soil has a higher humus content than desert soil. Give a reason. (iii) At which stage of decomposition are earthworms and centipedes involved? (iv) The net annual primary productivity (NPP) of a wetland ecosystem is 8,000 kcal/m² per year. Respiration by aquatic producers is 11,000 kcal/m² per year. Calculate the gross primary productivity (GPP).
modelAnswer:
(i) Breaking down of complex organic matter (decomposition) is essential because it releases inorganic nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, minerals) back into the soil and atmosphere. Without decomposition, nutrients would remain locked in dead organic matter, making them unavailable to producers, and the nutrient cycle would stop. It thus recycles matter and maintains nutrient availability for primary producers.

(ii) Forest soil has higher humus content than desert soil because forests have greater litter fall (leaves, branches, animal remains) and higher moisture levels. The warm, moist conditions in forests support abundant decomposer organisms (bacteria, fungi, earthworms) that efficiently break down organic matter to form humus. Desert soil is dry, hot, and has minimal litter and few decomposers, so very little humus accumulates.

(iii) Earthworms and centipedes are involved in fragmentation — the first stage of decomposition. They physically break the leaf litter and dead organic matter into smaller fragments, increasing the surface area for microbial decomposition.

(iv) GPP = NPP + Respiration by producers
GPP = 8,000 + 11,000 = 19,000 kcal/m² per year
keyPoints: Decomposition recycles nutrients for producers
Forest: more litter + moisture + decomposers → more humus; Desert: dry, little litter
Earthworms/centipedes: fragmentation stage; GPP = NPP + R = 8000 + 11000 = 19,000 kcal/m²/yr

subject: Biology
text: F. Griffith conducted a series of experiments on mice with two different strains of the bacterium Diplococcus pneumoniae. (i) Describe the entire procedure of this experiment. (ii) Write the conclusion of this experiment. (iii) What would have been the result if both strains were first heat-killed, mixed, and then injected in the mice?
modelAnswer:
(i) Griffith's Transformation Experiment (1928):
Griffith used two strains of Diplococcus pneumoniae (now Streptococcus pneumoniae):
• S-strain (Smooth): Has polysaccharide capsule → virulent, kills mice → forms smooth colonies
• R-strain (Rough): No capsule → non-virulent, mice survive → forms rough colonies

Experiment steps:
1. Injected live S-strain into mice → Mice died (virulent)
2. Injected live R-strain into mice → Mice survived (non-virulent)
3. Injected heat-killed S-strain → Mice survived (dead bacteria are harmless)
4. Injected mixture of heat-killed S-strain + live R-strain → Mice DIED; live S-strain bacteria were recovered from dead mice

(ii) Conclusion: Some 'transforming principle' from the heat-killed S-strain had been transferred to the live R-strain, converting (transforming) it into virulent S-strain. Griffith concluded that the hereditary material (later identified as DNA by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty in 1944) could be transferred between bacteria.

(iii) If both strains (S and R) were first heat-killed, mixed, and then injected:
The mice would SURVIVE. Both strains are heat-killed, so there are no living bacteria of either type. Without any live bacteria, no infection can occur and no transformation is possible. The mice would not develop pneumonia.
keyPoints: 4 experiments: live S → death; live R → survive; heat-killed S → survive; heat-killed S + live R → death
Conclusion: transforming principle (DNA) from S-strain transforms R-strain to virulent S-strain
Both heat-killed: mice would survive — no live bacteria, no infection, no transformation

text: Akshay Shrivastav launched a biofertiliser called Navyakosh used on paddy fields. (i) How do you think the use of the biofertiliser, Navyakosh, benefitted the paddy field? (ii) Name the microbe that was used to create the biofertiliser, Navyakosh.

subject: Biology
text: The diagram shows a method of screening transformed bacterial cells (blue and white colonies on a plate). Explain how the differently coloured colonies help in identifying the transformed cells.
modelAnswer:
This is blue-white colony selection using the lacZ gene. In the vector, the foreign DNA is inserted into the lacZ gene (which encodes β-galactosidase). 
• Blue colonies: lacZ gene is intact → bacteria produce β-galactosidase → X-gal substrate is cleaved → blue colour. These are non-recombinants (no insert).
• White colonies: Foreign DNA has disrupted lacZ gene → no functional β-galactosidase → X-gal not cleaved → white colour. These are recombinants (cells that have taken up the insert).
Thus white colonies identify successfully transformed (recombinant) cells.
keyPoints: White colonies = recombinants (insert disrupts lacZ gene, no β-galactosidase)
Blue colonies = non-recombinants (intact lacZ, β-galactosidase turns X-gal blue)

subject: Biology
text: Explain biopiracy with the help of an example.
modelAnswer:
Biopiracy refers to the unauthorised and uncompensated exploitation of biological resources (plants, animals, microbes) or associated traditional knowledge of indigenous/local communities by multinational companies or developed nations, without sharing the benefits with those communities.
Example: The use of Basmati rice strains by US company RiceTec Inc., which filed patents on Basmati rice hybrids that were developed over generations by Indian farmers. India contested these patents as the varieties were derived from traditional Indian knowledge without due acknowledgement or compensation.
keyPoints: Biopiracy = unauthorised exploitation of biodiversity/traditional knowledge without benefit-sharing

subject: Biology
text: (i) An organism living at an extremely hot place is likely to have a high GC content in its DNA. Give a reason to explain. (ii) If you are given the exact quantity of G and T, how will you calculate the quantity of A and C in the DNA? Why is this not possible in the RNA molecule?
modelAnswer:
(i) G-C base pairs are held together by three hydrogen bonds, while A-T base pairs have only two hydrogen bonds. A higher GC content makes the DNA more stable (higher melting temperature) and resistant to denaturation at high temperatures. Therefore organisms in hot environments (thermophiles) have high GC content for thermal stability.

(ii) In double-stranded DNA, Chargaff's rules apply: A = T and G = C. Therefore:
• If T is given, A = T (Adenine equals Thymine)
• If G is given, C = G (Cytosine equals Guanine)

This is NOT possible in RNA because RNA is usually single-stranded. There is no complementary strand, so there is no obligatory base pairing. Therefore A ≠ U and G ≠ C in RNA.
keyPoints: GC pairs have 3 H-bonds vs 2 for AT → higher stability at high temperature
In DNA: A=T and G=C (Chargaff's rule); RNA is single-stranded so Chargaff's rule does not apply

subject: Biology
text: Michelle, a zookeeper, found that in a population of 1000 rabbits, 360 had long ears (LL), 150 had medium ears (Ll), and 490 had short ears (ll). (i) Calculate the frequency of rabbits with heterozygous traits. (ii) Name the principle applied to calculate the frequency of rabbits. (iii) The next generation had 400 rabbits: 336 with long ears and 64 with short ears. Give a reason to explain the change in gene frequencies in the new population.
modelAnswer:
(i) Frequency of heterozygous (Ll) rabbits = 150/1000 = 0.15 (15%)

(ii) The principle applied is the Hardy-Weinberg principle (Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium).

(iii) The next generation has only LL (336) and ll (64) — no heterozygotes (Ll = 0). The total population fell from 1000 to 400. This is a small population where random genetic drift (chance fluctuations in allele frequencies) can cause significant changes. Also, the allele frequencies have changed: new q² = 64/400 = 0.16, so q = 0.4; p = 0.6 (previously p = 0.3, q = 0.7). Such a drastic change in a small population is best explained by genetic drift (founder effect or bottleneck), as alleles may be lost or fixed by chance rather than natural selection.
keyPoints: Heterozygous frequency = 150/1000 = 15%
Principle: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Change due to genetic drift in small population (population decreased from 1000 to 400)

subject: Biology
text: Refer to the sewage treatment diagram with Tank A (primary treatment), Tank B (secondary treatment with aeration tank and second sedimentation), and Tank C (effluent). (i) State one difference between primary and secondary sewage treatment. (ii) Identify the tank in which flocs are added. (iii) What is the purpose of using microbes in sewage treatment?
modelAnswer:
(i) Primary treatment (Tank A) is a physical process involving removal of large debris, grit, and suspended solids by screening and sedimentation. Secondary treatment (Tank B) is a biological process in which microorganisms (bacteria) decompose dissolved organic matter in the effluent.

(ii) Flocs (masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments) are added/formed in the aeration tank — part of Tank B (secondary treatment).

(iii) Microbes are used in sewage treatment to decompose the organic matter (BOD reduction). They break down harmful organic compounds into simpler inorganic substances, reducing the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) of the effluent so it is safe to be discharged into rivers.
keyPoints: Primary = physical removal; Secondary = biological decomposition by microbes
Flocs are formed/added in the aeration tank (secondary treatment)
Microbes reduce BOD by decomposing organic matter

subject: Biology
text: Draw and explain the Logistic population growth curve.
modelAnswer:
The logistic growth curve (S-shaped / sigmoid curve) describes population growth when resources are limited.

Equation: dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, where N = population size, K = carrying capacity, r = intrinsic rate of natural increase.

Phases:
1. Lag phase: Initial slow growth as the population acclimatises.
2. Exponential (log) phase: Rapid growth as resources are plentiful; population increases steeply.
3. Deceleration phase: Growth rate slows as population approaches K.
4. Plateau (stationary) phase: Growth rate becomes zero; population stabilises at K (carrying capacity).

The curve is S-shaped because intraspecific competition for limited resources increases as population grows, eventually limiting further growth.
keyPoints: S-shaped / sigmoid curve described by dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K
Phases: lag → exponential → deceleration → plateau at K
Population stabilises at carrying capacity K due to limited resources and intraspecific competition

subject: Biology
text: Draw a neat and well-labelled diagram of T.S. of mammalian testis.
modelAnswer:
A transverse section of the mammalian testis shows:
• Tunica albuginea: Outer fibrous capsule enclosing the testis.
• Septa: Connective tissue partitions dividing the testis into lobules.
• Seminiferous tubules: Highly coiled tubules within each lobule where spermatogenesis occurs. Their walls contain Sertoli cells (nurse cells) and spermatogenic cells (spermatogonia, primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa).
• Leydig cells (Interstitial cells): Present in the connective tissue between seminiferous tubules; secrete testosterone.
• Rete testis: Network of tubules connecting seminiferous tubules to the epididymis.
• Blood vessels and lymphatics: Present in the connective tissue.
[Diagram should show labelled seminiferous tubules, Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, tunica albuginea]
keyPoints: Tunica albuginea, septa, lobules with seminiferous tubules
Sertoli cells in tubule wall; Leydig cells in interstitial tissue (secrete testosterone)
Rete testis connects to epididymis

subject: Biology
text: (i) What is the role of restriction endonucleases in rDNA technology? (ii) A biotechnologist was given two restriction endonucleases (RE-A and RE-B) with restriction sites: RE-A cuts 5'GATATC3'/3'CTATAG5' (blunt ends) and RE-B cuts 5'G↓AATTC3'/3'CTTAA↑G5' (sticky ends). Draw the separated fragments produced after each enzyme's action.
modelAnswer:
(i) Restriction endonucleases are molecular scissors in rDNA technology. They recognise specific palindromic sequences (restriction sites) on DNA and cut it at precise positions. They produce either blunt ends or sticky ends (cohesive ends). Sticky ends facilitate the ligation of the desired gene into a vector by complementary base pairing before ligation with DNA ligase.

(ii) RE-A (blunt ends):
5'-GATAT   C-3'
3'-C   TATAG-5'
(Produces blunt-ended fragments with no overhangs)

RE-B (sticky ends):
5'-G          AATTC-3'
3'-CTTAA          G-5'
Fragments:
5'-G-3' with 3'-CTTAA-5' overhang (5' overhang: AATT)
5'-AATTC-3' with 3'-G-5' (5' overhang: AATT on other fragment)
(Produces 4-nucleotide 5' sticky ends: ...G + AATTC...)
keyPoints: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences; sticky ends facilitate gene cloning
RE-A: blunt ends (GATAT|C); RE-B: 5' sticky ends (G|AATTC produces AATT overhangs)

subject: Biology
text: Draw a neat flowchart depicting the life cycle of a retrovirus in the infected human cell.
modelAnswer:
Retrovirus life cycle in human cell:

1. HIV (retrovirus) attaches to CD4+ receptor on T-lymphocyte via gp120 glycoprotein
↓
2. Fusion of viral envelope with cell membrane; viral core (RNA + reverse transcriptase) enters cytoplasm
↓
3. Reverse transcription: Reverse transcriptase synthesises single-stranded DNA from viral RNA template
↓
4. Second DNA strand synthesised → double-stranded viral DNA (dsDNA) formed
↓
5. dsDNA enters nucleus and integrates into host chromosome as provirus (by integrase enzyme)
↓
6. Provirus transcribed by host RNA polymerase → viral RNA (genomic RNA + mRNA)
↓
7. Translation of viral mRNA → viral proteins (structural proteins, enzymes)
↓
8. Assembly: new viral RNA + proteins assemble at cell membrane
↓
9. Budding: New retrovirus particles bud off from cell membrane (acquiring lipid envelope)
↓
10. Mature HIV virions released to infect new CD4+ cells
keyPoints: Key step: reverse transcription (RNA → DNA) by reverse transcriptase; unique to retroviruses
Integration as provirus → transcription → translation → assembly → budding

subject: Biology
text: (a) Discuss any three contrivances for prevention of self-pollination in flowering plants. (b) State two differences between Apomixis and Polyembryony.
modelAnswer:
(a) Three contrivances for prevention of self-pollination:
1. Dichogamy: Anthers and stigma of a flower mature at different times. If anthers mature before stigma, it is protandry (e.g., sunflower, maize); if stigma matures first, it is protogyny (e.g., magnolia). This ensures pollen from the same flower is not available when the stigma is receptive.

2. Herkogamy: Physical structural barriers prevent self-pollination. Anthers and stigma are positioned such that self-deposition of pollen is impossible (e.g., in Calotropis, the stigma is shielded; in Iris, stigma is in a separate position from anthers).

3. Self-incompatibility (Self-sterility): The pollen of a flower fails to germinate on the stigma of the same plant due to biochemical rejection mechanisms controlled by the S-locus (e.g., Nicotiana, Petunia). The pollen tube is inhibited from growing even if pollen lands on the stigma.

(b) Differences between Apomixis and Polyembryony:
| Feature | Apomixis | Polyembryony |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Development of seeds/embryo without fertilisation | Formation of more than one embryo in a single seed |
| Fertilisation | Does not involve fertilisation | May involve both fertilised and unfertilised embryos |
| Genetic variation | No genetic variation; offspring are identical to mother | Offspring may show variation if multiple embryos arise differently |
| Example | Dandelion (Taraxacum), grasses | Citrus (oranges), Opuntia |
keyPoints: Three contrivances: dichogamy (different maturation times), herkogamy (structural barriers), self-incompatibility (biochemical rejection)
Apomixis: no fertilisation, genetically identical offspring; Polyembryony: multiple embryos per seed, may have fertilisation

subject: Biology
text: (i) Explain the Rivet Popper Hypothesis. [3] (ii) Briefly discuss the narrowly utilitarian and broadly utilitarian arguments for conserving biodiversity. [2]
modelAnswer:
(i) Rivet Popper Hypothesis (proposed by Paul Ehrlich):
This hypothesis compares the functioning of an ecosystem to the functioning of an aeroplane. Just as an aeroplane is held together by many rivets, an ecosystem is held together by many species. If some rivets are removed (species are lost), the aeroplane (ecosystem) continues to function, but further loss of rivets (extinction of more species) eventually causes catastrophic failure (ecosystem collapse). Each species plays a role — even if that role seems unimportant, the loss of too many species will destabilise the entire ecosystem. The hypothesis highlights that species cannot be lost without ultimately threatening the integrity of the ecosystem.

(ii) Utilitarian arguments for biodiversity conservation:

Narrowly Utilitarian: Biodiversity provides direct economic/tangible benefits to humans:
• Food crops (rice, wheat, fruits) and domestic animals are derived from wild species.
• Many medicines are derived from plants (quinine from Cinchona, morphine from Poppy, taxol from Taxus).
• Industrial products: fibres, dyes, resins, rubber, wood, gums are obtained from biodiversity.

Broadly Utilitarian: Biodiversity provides indirect, ecosystem-level services:
• Oxygen production and carbon fixation (climate regulation)
• Pollination of crops and natural vegetation
• Soil formation and nutrient cycling
• Water purification and flood control
• Aesthetic and recreational value (ecotourism)
keyPoints: Rivet Popper: species loss = removing rivets; ecosystem eventually collapses like an aeroplane losing too many rivets
Narrow utilitarian: direct economic benefits (food, medicine, fibre); Broad utilitarian: ecosystem services (pollination, climate, nutrient cycling)

subject: Biology
text: Rafiq, a ten-year-old boy, injured himself and could not stop bleeding. His uncle had died from the same condition. A genetic analysis showed Rafiq's mother and paternal grandmother are carriers of Bleeder's disease. (i) Draw a single pedigree chart to show the pattern of inheritance in Rafiq's family. (ii) What kind of inheritance pattern prevails in Rafiq's family? (iii) What are the chances of (a) Farah (Rafiq's sister) suffering from the same disease? (b) Farah being a carrier of the same disease?
modelAnswer:
(i) Pedigree chart (described textually):
Generation I: Paternal grandfather (normal, ○□) × Paternal grandmother (carrier, ○• with dot)
Generation II: Father (normal, □) × Mother (carrier, ○•); Father's brother (affected, ■)
Generation III: Rafiq (affected, ■), Farah (female, ○ - status to determine)
[In the pedigree: squares = males, circles = females; filled = affected; half-filled/dot = carrier]

(ii) The inheritance pattern is X-linked recessive inheritance (haemophilia/Bleeder's disease).
• Bleeder's disease is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome.
• Males (XY) with the recessive allele (X^h Y) are affected.
• Females are carriers (X^H X^h) if they have one normal allele and rarely affected.

(iii) Cross: Father (X^H Y, normal) × Mother (X^H X^h, carrier)
Possible offspring:
• Daughters: X^H X^H (normal, 1/2) or X^H X^h (carrier, 1/2)
• Sons: X^H Y (normal, 1/2) or X^h Y (affected, 1/2)

(a) Chance of Farah suffering from Bleeder's disease:
Farah is a daughter. Father can only give X^H to daughters. Mother gives X^H or X^h. For Farah to be affected, she would need X^h X^h (both X chromosomes recessive), but father gives only X^H. Therefore, Farah CANNOT be affected. Probability = 0 (zero).

(b) Chance of Farah being a carrier:
Farah's genotype is either X^H X^H or X^H X^h (always gets X^H from father). From mother (carrier X^H X^h), she gets X^H (50%) or X^h (50%). Therefore P(carrier) = 50% (1/2).
keyPoints: X-linked recessive inheritance (haemophilia)
Farah cannot be affected (father provides X^H to all daughters) → probability 0
Farah has 50% chance of being a carrier (inherits X^h from carrier mother with 50% probability)

subject: Biology
text: The diagram shows DNA banding patterns (gel electrophoresis) of a crime scene sample (C) and three suspects (S₁, S₂, S₃). (i) Which suspect's DNA sample matches the sample from the crime scene? (ii) Mention the principle on which DNA profiling is based.
modelAnswer:
(i) From the banding pattern, Suspect S₁ has bands at the same levels as the crime scene sample C. Therefore, S₁'s DNA matches the crime scene sample.

(ii) DNA profiling (DNA fingerprinting) is based on the principle of Variable Number Tandem Repeats (VNTRs) — also called Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) or mini/micro-satellites. These are specific regions of the DNA where short nucleotide sequences are repeated a variable number of times. The number and size of these repeats is unique to every individual (except identical twins), so the banding pattern on a gel acts as a unique fingerprint for each person.
keyPoints: Suspect S₁ matches the crime scene
Principle: Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTRs) / STRs — unique repetitive sequences in DNA vary between individuals

subject: Biology
text: In a group discussion, Shubham argued that Cleistogamy was a type of Xenogamy, whereas Ameena was of the opinion that it was a kind of Autogamy. Whose argument is correct? Justify.
modelAnswer:
Ameena's argument is correct. Cleistogamy is a type of Autogamy (self-pollination).

Justification: In cleistogamous flowers, the flower never opens (remains closed). The anthers dehisce and pollen grains are deposited on the stigma of the same closed flower — this is self-pollination (autogamy). Since pollination occurs within the same flower without the flower opening, it is a form of self-pollination/autogamy. It is NOT xenogamy (cross-pollination between different plants). Examples: Viola (violet), Commelina. Cleistogamy guarantees seed set even when pollinators are absent.
keyPoints: Ameena is correct — cleistogamy is autogamy (self-pollination in closed flowers)
Flowers never open; anthers deposit pollen on stigma of same flower; guaranteed seed set without pollinators

subject: Biology
text: In the food chain Grass → Zebra → Crocodile → Vulture, the amount of energy at the fourth trophic level (Vulture) is 4 J. What will be the amount of energy available at the sunlight/transducer level (Grass)?
modelAnswer:
Using the 10% energy transfer law (Lindeman's law):

4th trophic level (Vulture) = 4 J
3rd trophic level (Crocodile) = 4 × 10 = 40 J
2nd trophic level (Zebra) = 40 × 10 = 400 J
1st trophic level (Grass/transducer) = 400 × 10 = 4,000 J

Sunlight input to producers (assuming ~10% photosynthetic efficiency) = 4,000 × 10 = 40,000 J

The transducer level (Grass/producers) = 4,000 J; Sunlight = 40,000 J
keyPoints: 4th trophic = 4 J → Grass (transducer) = 4,000 J (reverse of 10% law, ×10 per level going back)
Sunlight = 40,000 J (producers fix ~10% of PAR)

subject: Biology
text: Anthony needs to produce a specific biological product in large quantities. His lab has two vessels — one with a sparger and one with a stirrer. Which vessel will be more advantageous for Anthony? Why?
modelAnswer:
The vessel with a sparger will be more advantageous for Anthony.

Reason: A sparger introduces sterile air/oxygen as fine bubbles into the culture medium, ensuring proper aeration. Most biological products (enzymes, antibiotics, vitamins) are produced by aerobic microorganisms that need a continuous oxygen supply. The sparger maintains dissolved oxygen levels in the medium, supporting microbial growth and product formation.

A stirrer alone provides mixing but does not supply oxygen. Without adequate oxygen, aerobic production would be limited. Therefore, the vessel with the sparger is more advantageous for large-scale production of a biological product.
keyPoints: Sparger vessel is better — provides oxygen (aeration) via fine bubbles
Most biological products require aerobic conditions; sparger maintains dissolved O₂ for microbial growth

subject: Biology
text: Data shows a decline in migratory bird population in a Southern Indian wetland (2023: 10,000 birds, 85% aquatic plants, 350 ha; 2024: 8,000 birds, 60% plants, 280 ha; 2025: 5,000 birds, 45% plants, 220 ha). Interpret two reasons for the change in population of migratory birds.
modelAnswer:
Two reasons for the decline in migratory bird population:

1. Decline in aquatic plant cover (from 85% to 45%): Aquatic plants serve as nesting sites, shelter, and food sources (seeds, insects on plants) for migratory birds. Reduction in plant cover means less food and habitat availability, leading to fewer birds visiting.

2. Reduction in aquatic area (from 350 ha to 220 ha): The wetland area has shrunk, likely due to drainage, encroachment or human activity. A smaller aquatic area means reduced habitat space, fewer feeding grounds and reduced carrying capacity for the birds, resulting in population decline.
keyPoints: Decline in aquatic plants → less food, shelter and nesting sites for birds
Reduction in wetland area → less habitat/feeding ground, lower carrying capacity

subject: Biology
text: Paramecium caudatum and Paramecium aurelia were growing separately but when placed in the same medium, P. caudatum got eliminated. Identify and explain the type of ecological interaction on the basis of Gause's principle.
modelAnswer:
The interaction is Interspecific Competition. Based on Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle: when two species compete for exactly the same limited resources (same ecological niche) in the same habitat, the more efficient competitor will eventually outcompete and eliminate the other.

In this case, P. aurelia outcompeted P. caudatum (because P. aurelia is a better competitor for the same food/resources in the shared medium), leading to the exclusion (elimination) of P. caudatum. Both species occupy the same niche — hence competitive exclusion occurs. This demonstrates that two species with identical ecological niches cannot coexist indefinitely.
keyPoints: Interspecific competition; Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle
P. aurelia outcompetes P. caudatum for the same niche resources; two species cannot coexist on the same limiting resource

subject: Biology
text: (i) A plasmid without a selectable marker was used as the vector for gene cloning. Predict the outcome of this experiment. (ii) Name an artificial chromosome that can be used as a vector to transfer recombinant DNA in Penicillium notatum.
modelAnswer:
(i) Outcome: Without a selectable marker (antibiotic resistance gene or other selection gene), it will be impossible to distinguish between host cells that have taken up the recombinant plasmid and those that have not. All colonies — transformed and non-transformed — will look identical. There is no way to screen for recombinant cells, making it impossible to identify and select cells that contain the desired cloned gene. The experiment will fail to identify successful transformants.

(ii) YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosome) — Wait, Penicillium is a fungus (similar to yeast). The appropriate artificial chromosome for fungal transformation would be a YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosome) or more specifically for filamentous fungi, an AMA1-based ARS plasmid. However, in ISC context, the answer is YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosome), as Penicillium is a eukaryotic fungus.
keyPoints: No selectable marker → cannot distinguish transformants from non-transformants; experiment fails to identify recombinants
Artificial chromosome for Penicillium (fungus): YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosome)

subject: Biology
text: (i) How is mature insulin different from proinsulin secreted by pancreas in humans? (ii) Name the company that produced genetically engineered insulin for the first time. (iii) Why is functional insulin produced by rDNA technology better than the ones produced earlier?
modelAnswer:
(i) Proinsulin is a single polypeptide chain containing three segments: A chain, B chain, and a connecting C-peptide. To become mature (functional) insulin, the C-peptide is enzymatically cleaved off, leaving the A-chain and B-chain connected by two disulphide bonds. Mature insulin is therefore shorter and has no C-peptide.

(ii) Eli Lilly (USA) produced genetically engineered human insulin (Humulin) for the first time in 1982, using recombinant DNA technology with E. coli.

(iii) Advantages of rDNA technology-produced insulin:
• It produces human insulin (identical to endogenous insulin), so it causes fewer allergic reactions compared to previously used animal insulin (from pigs/cows) which had slight structural differences.
• Animal insulin (porcine/bovine) could trigger immune reactions and had limited supply; rDNA insulin is human-identical and can be produced in unlimited quantities.
• Eliminates the risk of animal-derived contaminants and ensures consistent purity.
keyPoints: Proinsulin has C-peptide; mature insulin: C-peptide removed, A+B chains held by disulphide bonds
First produced by Eli Lilly (Humulin, 1982)
rDNA insulin = human insulin → fewer allergies than animal insulin; unlimited supply; no animal-derived impurities

subject: Biology
text: A biologist surveyed islands: P (1 km², 5 species), Q (10 km², 18 species), R (100 km², 60 species), S (1000 km², 150 species). (i) What pattern is observed? (ii) Name the scientist who proposed the concept of relationship between area and species. (iii) Write the mathematical expression for this relationship.
modelAnswer:
(i) Pattern: As the island area increases, the number of mammalian species also increases. Larger islands support more species. This is the species-area relationship (species richness increases with area). The relationship is not linear but follows a power law (logarithmic relationship).

(ii) The species-area relationship was first proposed by Alexander von Humboldt (observed the pattern). It was later mathematically formulated by Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson (Theory of Island Biogeography).

(iii) Mathematical expression:
log S = log C + Z log A
Or equivalently: S = C × A^Z
Where: S = species richness, A = area of the island/region, Z = regression coefficient (slope of the log-log plot, typically 0.1–0.2 for smaller areas, 0.6–1.2 for continents), C = Y-intercept (related to the number of species at unit area).
keyPoints: Pattern: species richness increases with island area (species-area relationship)
Alexander von Humboldt (observed); MacArthur and Wilson (mathematical formulation)
S = C × A^Z (or log S = log C + Z log A)

subject: Biology
text: (i) Draw a flowchart to show the process of sex determination in honeybees. (ii) If there are 16 chromosomes in the somatic cells of a male honeybee, how many chromosomes would be present in spermatozoa?
modelAnswer:
(i) Sex determination in honeybees (haplo-diploid system):

Queen (2n = 32, diploid)
├─ Lays FERTILISED eggs (by stored sperm from drone)
│   └─→ Diploid larvae (2n) → Fed royal jelly → Queen (fertile female)
│                           → Fed worker jelly → Worker bees (sterile females)
└─ Lays UNFERTILISED eggs (parthenogenesis)
    └─→ Haploid larvae (n) → Drone (male)

Males (drones) are produced from unfertilised eggs by parthenogenesis; they are haploid.
Females (queens and workers) develop from fertilised eggs; they are diploid.

(ii) If somatic cells of male honeybee (drone) have 16 chromosomes, the drone is haploid (n = 16). Since drones are haploid, they produce spermatozoa by mitosis (not meiosis). Therefore, spermatozoa also contain 16 chromosomes (same as somatic cells).
keyPoints: Haplo-diploid: fertilised eggs → diploid females; unfertilised eggs → haploid males (drones)
Male somatic = 16 chromosomes (haploid n=16); drones produce sperm by mitosis → spermatozoa = 16 chromosomes

subject: Biology
text: The chemical structure shown (with two OH groups and pentyl chain on a terpenophenolic ring system) is an addictive drug. (i) Mention the scientific name of the source plant. (ii) State any one effect of this drug on the human body. (iii) What is meant by withdrawal symptom?
modelAnswer:
(i) The drug is cannabidiol (CBD) or THC (tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabinol), derived from Cannabis sativa (marijuana/hemp plant).

(ii) Effect on the human body: Causes psychedelic/hallucinogenic effects — alters perception, causes euphoria, relaxation, slowed reaction time, increased appetite, distorted sense of time, and impaired short-term memory. At high doses, may cause paranoia and anxiety.

(iii) Withdrawal symptom: The unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that appear when a person who is addicted to a drug suddenly stops taking it or significantly reduces their dose. Withdrawal symptoms of Cannabis include: irritability, anxiety, insomnia, decreased appetite, restlessness, and mood swings. These occur because the body has become dependent on the drug and struggles to function normally without it.

Effect: psychedelic/hallucinogenic — euphoria, altered perception, impaired memory
Withdrawal symptom: unpleasant symptoms on stopping an addictive drug; Cannabis withdrawal: irritability, insomnia, anxiety

subject: Biology
text: A researcher compares two embryos: Embryo X (equal first division of zygote, two identical cells) and Embryo Y (unequal first division — small apical cell and large basal cell). (i) Which embryo is likely to develop into a normal dicot embryo? (ii) What is the fate of (a) the apical cell and (b) the basal cell?
modelAnswer:
(i) Embryo Y (with unequal first division producing a small apical cell and a large basal cell) is likely to develop into a normal dicot embryo. In dicotyledons, the first division of the zygote is characteristically asymmetrical/unequal, producing a small terminal (apical) cell and a large basal cell.

(ii) Fate of the cells:
(a) Apical cell: The small apical cell undergoes repeated mitotic divisions to form the embryo proper (the main body of the embryo, which includes the cotyledons, epicotyl, hypocotyl, and radicle).
(b) Basal cell: The large basal cell divides to form the suspensor — a multicellular structure that anchors the embryo within the embryo sac and channels nutrients from the surrounding tissue to the developing embryo. The lowermost cell of the suspensor may become the hypophysis (forms the root cap and rootlet tip).
keyPoints: Embryo Y (unequal division) develops into a normal dicot embryo
Apical cell → embryo proper (cotyledons, epicotyl, hypocotyl, radicle); Basal cell → suspensor (anchors and nourishes embryo)

subject: Biology
text: A graph shows antibody levels after first infection (Peak A, weeks 1-4) and second infection (Peak B, higher, weeks 7-9). (a) What types of responses of the immune system do peaks A and B represent? (b) Name the type of antibody at highest level in the 7th week.
modelAnswer:
(a) Peak A represents the Primary Immune Response: This is the first time the immune system encounters the antigen. It is slower (lag period of 1-2 weeks), produces a lower peak level of antibodies, and is mainly IgM antibodies. Memory cells are also formed during this phase.

Peak B represents the Secondary Immune Response (anamnestic response): On second exposure to the same antigen, memory B cells (formed during primary response) are rapidly activated and proliferate. The response is faster (no lag), produces much higher levels of antibodies (higher Peak B), and predominantly IgG antibodies with longer-lasting protection.

(b) At the 7th week, which is shortly after the second infection (starting ~week 7), the antibody at highest level is IgG (Immunoglobulin G). The secondary response produces predominantly IgG which is more effective and longer-lasting.
keyPoints: Peak A = Primary immune response (slow, lower, mainly IgM, first exposure)
Peak B = Secondary immune response (faster, higher, memory cells activated)
7th week: IgG antibody at highest level (secondary response predominance)

subject: Biology
text: Two structures are shown in spermatogenesis: Structure A (a rounded spermatid) and Structure B (a mature spermatozoon). (i) Identify the process which converts Structure A to Structure B. (ii) State any two modifications observable in Structure B compared to A.
modelAnswer:
(i) The process that converts a spermatid (Structure A) into a spermatozoon (Structure B) is Spermiogenesis (also called spermateliosis or sperm morphogenesis).

(ii) Two modifications observable in Structure B (spermatozoon) compared to Structure A (spermatid):
1. Loss of cytoplasm: The bulk of the cytoplasm is shed as a residual body; the spermatozoon has very little cytoplasm compared to the rounded spermatid.
2. Formation of flagellum: A long flagellum (tail) develops from one of the centrioles, enabling motility — the spermatid has no tail.
(Other modifications: condensation and elongation of nucleus; formation of acrosome from Golgi apparatus; mitochondria arrange around the mid-piece for energy supply.)
keyPoints: Process: Spermiogenesis
Modifications: loss of cytoplasm; formation of flagellum/tail; acrosome formation; nuclear condensation/elongation; mid-piece mitochondria

subject: Biology
text: Arun studied locusts in a forest over 35 days: Day 1: 5, Day 2: 10, Day 5: 25, Day 10: 50, Day 15: 105, Day 20: 170, Day 25: 280, Day 30: 360, Day 35: 200. (i) Construct a growth curve from this data. What type of growth curve is obtained? (ii) Write a mathematical expression for the growth curve obtained.
modelAnswer:
(i) Plotting the data shows population increasing rapidly from Day 1 to Day 30, reaching a peak of 360 at Day 30, then declining to 200 at Day 35. This describes a boom-and-bust pattern. The rising portion (Days 1–30) resembles a J-shaped (exponential) growth curve, but the decline after Day 30 makes it a bell-shaped or boom-bust curve rather than a pure logistic curve. The overall shape resembles a logistic (S-shaped) curve that overshoots and declines — typical of many insect populations.

Conclusion: The growth curve obtained is a J-shaped (exponential) curve for the initial phase (Days 1–25) followed by a decline — representing a boom-and-bust population cycle.

(ii) For the exponential phase (Days 1–25):
dN/dt = rN
(where N = number of locusts, r = intrinsic rate of natural increase, t = time)

For the overall curve (if treating as logistic before the crash):
dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K
(where K = carrying capacity)
keyPoints: Growth curve: initially J-shaped (exponential) followed by decline (boom-bust cycle); peaks at Day 30 = 360 then falls
Mathematical expression: dN/dt = rN (exponential phase); or dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K (logistic phase)

subject: Biology
text: A diagram shows DNA strands A and C with +1 marking, a 'synthesis' arrow, and parts labelled E and F. (i) Identify the parts marked E and F. (ii) Explain the post-transcriptional modifications that occur in part F.
modelAnswer:
(i) Identification:
• Part E: The promoter region / transcription start site (+1). This is the region on the template DNA strand (strand C) just upstream of the +1 (start) site where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. (Specifically, E appears to be the sigma factor/RNA polymerase binding site — the promoter sequence including the TATA box in eukaryotes.)
• Part F: The primary RNA transcript (hnRNA / pre-mRNA) — the newly synthesised RNA molecule produced from the template DNA strand. In eukaryotes, this is the heterogeneous nuclear RNA that is then processed.

(ii) Post-transcriptional modifications of pre-mRNA (hnRNA — part F) in eukaryotes:

1. 5' Capping: A 7-methyl guanosine (m7G) cap is added to the 5' end of the pre-mRNA. This protects the mRNA from degradation by exonucleases, helps in ribosome attachment during translation, and aids in nuclear export.

2. 3' Polyadenylation: A poly-A tail (a string of 200–250 adenine nucleotides) is added to the 3' end of the pre-mRNA. This protects the mRNA from 3' degradation and aids in nuclear export and translation.

3. Splicing: Introns (non-coding intervening sequences) are excised/removed from the pre-mRNA by spliceosomes (small nuclear RNP complexes). The remaining exons are joined together to form the mature mRNA (continuous coding sequence). This produces the final translatable mRNA.
keyPoints: E = promoter/transcription start site; F = primary RNA transcript (hnRNA/pre-mRNA)
Post-transcriptional modifications: (1) 5' capping with m7G cap; (2) 3' poly-A tail addition; (3) Splicing — removal of introns by spliceosome, joining of exons

subject: Biology
text: (i) Outline three major steps in the process of artificial hybridisation. (ii) Discuss the role of pollen-pistil interaction in ensuring successful hybrid formation. OR (iii) Draw a flowchart to represent the process of oogenesis. (iv) Differentiate between oogenesis and spermatogenesis on the basis of: (a) Number of products (b) Gonadal hormones.
modelAnswer:
(i) Three major steps in artificial hybridisation:
1. Emasculation: Removal of anthers from the flower of the female parent (before they mature/dehisce) using forceps to prevent self-pollination. This step ensures the female parent does not fertilise itself.
2. Bagging: After emasculation, the flower is covered with a paper/polythene bag to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen from other sources. The bag isolates the stigma until it is ready for pollination.
3. Rebagging after pollination: When the stigma becomes receptive, the bag is removed, pollen from the desired male parent is dusted/applied onto the stigma, and the flower is rebagged to prevent further contamination. The seed/fruit is then allowed to develop.

(ii) Role of pollen-pistil interaction:
Pollen-pistil interaction ensures compatibility (successful fertilisation) between the pollen and pistil:
• Recognition: The stigma surface recognises compatible pollen via specific glycoproteins and proteins on the pollen wall. Compatible pollen germinates; incompatible pollen is rejected.
• Germination: Compatible pollen grains absorb water and nutrients from the stigma, causing the pollen tube to grow through the style.
• Pollen tube guidance: Chemical signals (chemotropism) from the ovule guide the pollen tube through the style to the embryo sac, ensuring the male gametes reach the egg cell for fertilisation.
• This selectivity ensures successful hybrid formation by allowing only the intended cross-compatible pollen to fertilise, preventing unwanted pollinations.

(OR: iii) Flowchart for oogenesis:
Oogonia (2n) [Fetal ovary]
↓ Mitosis (multiplication)
Primary oocyte (2n) [arrested in Prophase I — dictyotene stage at birth]
↓ Meiosis I resumes at puberty/each cycle
Secondary oocyte (n) + First polar body (n)
↓ Meiosis II begins (arrested at Metaphase II)
[If fertilisation occurs:]
↓ Meiosis II completion
Ovum (n) + Second polar body (n) → Fertilised ovum (zygote)

(iv) Differences:
(a) Number of products:
• Oogenesis: produces 1 functional ovum + 2-3 polar bodies (non-functional). Only one functional gamete per primary oocyte.
• Spermatogenesis: produces 4 functional spermatozoa per primary spermatocyte (all four are functional).

(b) Gonadal hormones:
• Oogenesis: regulated by oestrogen and progesterone (ovarian hormones; FSH and LH from pituitary stimulate oogenesis and ovulation).
• Spermatogenesis: regulated by testosterone (secreted by Leydig cells of testis; FSH and LH/ICSH stimulate spermatogenesis).
keyPoints: Artificial hybridisation: emasculation, bagging, controlled pollination + rebagging
Pollen-pistil interaction: recognition via surface proteins, compatible pollen germinates, pollen tube grows to ovule
Oogenesis: 1 ovum + polar bodies; regulated by oestrogen/progesterone. Spermatogenesis: 4 spermatozoa; regulated by testosterone
